articles.title: PF faz operação contra ex-servidor do STJ por vazamento de dados | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-secretário de TI do STJ, Humberto Pradera teria violado o sigilo funcional facilitando o acesso do advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio, a informações de processos na Corte.
articles.summary: A Operação Linceu apura se o ex-secretário Humberto Pradera facilitou o acesso de Willer Tomaz a informações sigilosas de processos em tramitação no STJ.
articles.body:
A Polícia Federal realizou nesta segunda-feira (19) uma operação para apurar possível violação de sigilo funcional por parte de Humberto Fontoura Pradera, um ex-servidor do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ).

O ex-servidor é suspeito de ter facilitado o acesso indevido do advogado Willer Tomaz a informações de processos em tramitação no STJ. Willer nega ter tido acesso irregular a dados sobre processos ( leia a íntegra da nota aqui ).

🔎O advogado Willer Tomaz é amigo do senador e candidato à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Willer e Flávio são investigados em um inquérito no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) sobre suposta lavagem de dinheiro . A operação da PF desta segunda foi determinada dentro desse inquérito.

Alvo da operação, Humberto Pradera ocupava o cargo em comissão de secretário de Tecnologia da Informação da Corte, do qual foi exonerado na última sexta-feira (16) pelo presidente do STJ, ministro Luís Felipe Salomão . O g1 não localizou o ex-servidor do STJ e sua defesa.

Os agentes da PF cumprem um mandado de busca e apreensão contra Pradera, em Brasília, determinado pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), relator do inquérito aberto no STF.

Batizada de Operação Linceu, a operação desta segunda apura a suposta prática dos seguintes crimes:

De acordo com apurações da Polícia Federal, que constam de um relatório elaborado pela corporação, Humberto Fontoura Pradera, então servidor da área de tecnologia do STJ, repassou ao advogado Willer Tomaz informações relacionadas a demandas internas do tribunal.

Em mensagens, Pradera contou a Willer que duas pessoas haviam sido designadas para tratar de determinado assunto e afirmou que manteria o advogado informado.

Outro episódio aponta que Pradera encaminhou uma fotografia de um documento exibido na tela de um computador, com um carimbo sobre a mesa.

Pradera ocupava uma posição de destaque no tribunal exercendo o cargo de secretário de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (STI).

Antes disso, também havia sido assessor-chefe da Assessoria de Inteligência Artificial do STJ, participando de projetos ligados à transformação digital, à inteligência artificial e aos sistemas internos do tribunal.

Em outra troca de mensagens que consta no documento, ao ser questionado por Willer sobre “qual o número deles?”, Pradera respondeu que “essa tá no REsp 2122969” e afirmou que a tutela teria perdido efeito em razão do julgamento.

Segundo os investigadores, a conversa mostra o compartilhamento de informações sobre o processo, acompanhado de explicações sobre seus possíveis efeitos.

🔎Em nota, o STJ afirmou que afastou e exonerou servidores suspeitos de irregularidades e vazamento de informações, abrindo processos administrativos para apurar possíveis infrações. O tribunal também disse que reforçou os protocolos de segurança interna e anunciou o lançamento do 'Programa Confiança Digital' para reduzir novos riscos tecnológicos e proteger dados institucionais.

Em relação ao que a PF já investigou sobre Willer Tomaz, no inquérito sobre suposta lavagem de dinheiro, os investigadores afirmam que a atuação dele se concentrava em dois eixos: financeiro e jurídico.

No plano financeiro, a Polícia Federal identificou movimentações de cerca de R$ 130 milhões no Magnum Bank entre março e maio de 2025, caracterizadas por grandes entradas seguidas de fracionamento, triangulações e repasses entre diversas empresas e plataformas de apostas, além de conexões com agentes políticos e servidores públicos.

No eixo jurídico, a investigação apontou uma suposta interferência em processos de alto interesse econômico no STJ e na PGR.

As investigações indicam que Willer recebia votos, ementas e decisões judiciais de forma antecipada, influenciando decisões como a desistência de recursos, além de enviar orientações e conteúdos para a elaboração de pareceres do Ministério Público Federal.

O advogado Willer Tomaz, alvo de inquérito no STF — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

Leia a íntegra da nota divulgada pelo advogado Willer Tomaz após a operação desta sexta-feira (19):

O advogado Willer Tomaz nega categoricamente ter tido acesso irregular ou não autorizado a decisões judiciais ou a pareceres do Ministério Público Federal, bem como ter interferido em qualquer manifestação. As insinuações são falsas, configuram desinformação e revelam desconhecimento elementar, ou deliberada distorção, do funcionamento dos tribunais.

A ciência antecipada de julgados no Superior Tribunal de Justiça não é crime: é funcionalidade prevista no próprio sistema da Corte. Tampouco há ilícito quando um procurador, convencido pelos memoriais apresentados, incorpora seus argumentos ao parecer. Isso é contraditório, e converter rotina processual em suspeita é criminalizar a advocacia.

A defesa desconhece o relatório citado e repudia sua divulgação seletiva, em plena campanha eleitoral, com menções a terceiros alheios aos fatos investigados. Ilegal, este sim, é o vazamento de material sigiloso, cujos autores serão identificados e responsabilizados.

articles.title: TSE informa mudança em 554 locais de votação do primeiro para o segundo turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao longo do fim de semana, número tem sofrido diversas alterações. TSE diz que as 'zonas eleitorais estão concluindo registros e ajustes necessários nos sitemas'.
articles.summary: Ao longo do fim de semana, número tem sofrido diversas alterações. TSE diz que as 'zonas eleitorais estão concluindo registros e ajustes necessários nos sitemas'.
articles.body:
Os sistemas do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) apontam, nesta segunda-feira (19), que 554 seções eleitorais apresentaram uma alteração no local de votação entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições deste ano.

As mudanças ocorreram em 22 estados e, juntos, os locais de votação alterados somam 163,6 mil eleitores.

Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, "os números ainda estão sendo atualizados à medida que as zonas eleitorais concluem os registros e ajustes necessários nos sistemas da Justiça Eleitoral, inclusive para refletir a manutenção, no segundo turno, de locais que haviam sido alterados provisoriamente no primeiro".

No próximo domingo (25), mais de 158 milhões de brasileiros devem votar no segundo turno das eleições para presidente da República. Em seis estados e no Distrito Federal, os eleitores também escolherão o governador.

➡️A orientação para o eleitor é que, antes de sair para votar, consulte o local de votação pelo aplicativo e-título ou pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral.

Uma resolução do TSE que disciplina os atos gerais das eleições de 2026 não estabelece uma data-limite para alterações nos locais de votação.

Segundo o tribunal, eventuais mudanças podem ocorrer até a data da votação, em último caso.

Entre os motivos para alterações estão situações climáticas extremas, problemas de infraestrutura e questões de segurança pública.

Ao longo do último fim de semana, os sistemas da Justiça Eleitoral apontavam números diferentes em relação ao número de locais de votação alterados.

A inconsistência fez com que o número de seções eleitorais efetivamente modificadas para o segundo turno fosse menor do que as 2.033 registradas na página oficial do tribunal no início da tarde deste domingo (18). Na sexta-feira (16), o TSE havia informado um número ainda maior, de 4,3 mil seções eleitorais alteradas.

Outra questão é a alteração de locais de votação provisórios no primeiro turno, que podem ser, ou não, mantidos. Isso ainda está em avaliação nas próprias zonas eleitorais.

Na manhã desta segunda (19), o número informado pela Justiça Eleitoral no sistema é 774. No início da manhã, era 1.106.

O TSE explica que a Justiça Eleitoral não determina mudanças em locais de votação.

"Essas decisões são tomadas no âmbito das próprias zonas eleitorais, que conhecem as peculiaridades de cada localidade, avaliam as condições dos imóveis e adotam as providências necessárias, observadas as normas da Justiça Eleitoral", informa, em nota.

TREs fazem força-tarefa para informar mudanças

Diante das inconsistências nos dados do TSE, os Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais estão fazendo uma força-tarefa para esclarecer quais locais realmente sofreram alterações, com publicações nos sites e nas redes sociais.

No Paraná, enquanto a página do TSE apontava alterações em 61 locais de votação de 48 municípios, o levantamento do TRE-PR identificou mudanças em apenas oito locais, em sete municípios.

Já em São Paulo, a página oficial do TSE apontava alterações em oito municípios, envolvendo 15 locais de votação. Mas o TRE-SP informou oficialmente mudanças apenas na 256ª Zona Eleitoral, no Tucuruvi, na capital, e na 402ª Zona Eleitoral, em Presidente Prudente.

No Rio de Janeiro, a página do TSE indicava mudanças em dois locais de votação, um na capital e outro em Nova Iguaçu, na Baixada Fluminense. O TRE-RJ, porém, informou que apenas um local de votação foi efetivamente alterado, no bairro de Brás de Pina, na Zona Norte da capital.

O TSE disse que as alterações nos locais de votação não são decididas de forma centralizada pelo órgão e que a responsabilidade cabe a cada zona eleitoral, que conhece a realidade de seu município e avalia a infraestrutura disponível.

articles.title: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro: Contraste de estilos marca primeiro debate | G1
articles.standfirst: Aliados avaliam que o presidente deixou de explorar temas sensíveis ao adversário, enquanto o senador impôs uma dinâmica voltada à repercussão nas redes.
articles.summary: O debate Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro revelou o contraste entre a política tradicional e a dinâmica das redes sociais nas eleições 2026.
articles.body:
Candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula participam de debate da Band antes do 2º turno das eleições. — Foto: REUTERS/Jean Carniel

Nos bastidores da campanha de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ), a avaliação de aliados é que o presidente perdeu a oportunidade de explorar temas considerados sensíveis para Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) no primeiro debate do segundo turno das eleições de 2026 .

Entre eles, a questão da licença-maternidade, o debate sobre a quebra de sigilo e os questionamentos envolvendo a compra de um imóvel na casa dos R$ 10 milhões. Para esses interlocutores, Lula deveria ter insistido nas cobranças e exigido explicações mais detalhadas do adversário — mas Flavio Bolsonaro conseguiu mudar a pauta.

Os candidatos à Presidência da República participaram na noite de domingo (18) do primeiro debate do segundo turno, promovido pelo Grupo Bandeirantes.

O debate também expôs um contraste de estilos e estratégias de comunicação: de um lado, um candidato mais analógico, acostumado ao confronto político tradicional; do outro, um candidato digital, influenciado pela linguagem de Donald Trump e Pablo Marçal, que aposta em provocações, frases de efeito e momentos com potencial de viralização nas redes sociais.

A avaliação nos bastidores é que a disputa não se limita mais ao desempenho diante das câmeras. Ela continua nas redes, onde cada resposta, ataque ou provocação pode ser transformado em cortes e conteúdo político. É justamente essa diferença de linguagem que também entrou no radar da campanha de Lula após o confronto.

No fim, o resumo é que ambos falaram para alimentar suas bolhas- sem garantias de que convenceram indecisos a votar.

articles.title: Lula expôs Flávio em casos de corrupção, e senador acertou ao deixar petista 'visivelmente irritado', avaliam aliados | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos discutiram segurança, economia, saúde e divergiram sobre maioridade penal e relação com os EUA; votação será no próximo domingo (25).
articles.summary: Candidatos discutiram segurança, economia, saúde e divergiram sobre maioridade penal e relação com os EUA; votação será no próximo domingo (25).
articles.body:
Debate da Band entre Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: Reuters/Jean Carniel

Integrantes das campanhas do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) avaliaram, nesta segunda-feira (19), que eles foram bem no primeiro debate na televisão, que foi ao ar neste domingo (18).

Enquanto o coordenador da campanha petista, Edinho Silva, avalia que o presidente conseguiu expor o envolvimento de Flávio com casos de corrupção, a equipe do senador diz que ele acertou ao deixar Lula “visivelmente irritado”, mas que precisa apresentar mais propostas no debate da TV Globo , na próxima sexta (23).

Segundo Edinho Silva, Lula foi bem ao expor os escândalos envolvendo Flávio Bolsonaro e se saiu bem das perguntas do adversário envolvendo a lobista Roberta Luchsinger e seu filho Fábio Luiz, o Lulinha, ao desafiar Flávio a abrir seu sigilo bancário.

"Presidente Lula conseguiu mostrar ao país quem é Flávio Bolsonaro. Um político profissional que dezenas de anos de mandatos e um currículo trágico. Defende miliciano, defendeu assassinos, e propôs projetos que beneficiam o crime organizado, votou contra ampliar a licença-maternidade na Alerj, foi contra o fim da escala 6x1 e está envolvido em todas as demovias de corrupção do último período", afirmou Edinho.

O coordenador da campanha de Lula rechaça que ele foi desestabilizado por Flávio e garante que o petista seguirá a estratégia no debate da TV Globo , marcado para a próxima sexta-feira (23).

"Vamos continuar mostrando quem é Flávio Bolsonaro e fazer o confronto de projetos. Quem não quer discutir propostas é o Flávio porque ele não tem", pontuou.

Aliado de primeira hora de Lula, o senador Otto Alencar (PSD-BA) avalia que Flávio teve uma postura infantil no debate. O parlamentar ironizou a estratégia inspirada no presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, de ficar atrás do petista enquanto ele falava para as câmeras.

"Ele ficou de forma jocosa atrás do presidente. Mas ali para mim já é premonição, já que ele vai chegar atrás no dia 25. Já fica por ali mesmo", ironizou Alencar.

Para o senador, Flávio se recusou a responder as perguntas de Lula e destacou que ele não aceitou o desafio de abrir o sigilo bancário feito pelo petista.

"Ele não aceitou o desafio que todo político devia aceitar, que era abrir o sigilo bancário e fiscal. Não aceitou e não respondeu" .

Campanha de Flávio comemora, mas aliados querem propostas

Após o debate, integrantes da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro se reuniram para avaliar o desempenho do candidato do PL à Presidência.

Segundo interlocutores do senador, em linhas gerais, a avaliação é que Flávio se saiu bem e foi “excelente” ao conseguir deixar o presidente Lula, candidato do PT à reeleição, “muito nervoso” e “rabugento” em alguns momentos, quando confrontado sobre temas como as suspeitas sobre o filho Fábio Luís da Silva, conhecido como Lulinha.

Para a cúpula da campanha, Flávio “dominou” o estilo do debate, principalmente no momento em que os dois puderam discutir livremente por 30 minutos, sem tema definido e com um respondendo ao outro.

Líder do PL na Câmara, o deputado Sóstenes Cavalcante (RJ) também avaliou como positiva a participação de Flávio, pois atingiu o “objetivo”, que, segundo ele, era “deixar o Lula visivelmente irritado”.

Entretanto, para o aliado de Flávio, o candidato do PL precisa usar o próximo debate, na TV Globo, na próxima sexta (23), para apresentar mais propostas para um eventual governo, caso seja eleito.

"O Flávio tentou apresentar propostas, conseguiu poucas", afirmou Sóstenes.

Para Sóstenes, Lula acabou cometendo erros, como dizer que quer votos de presos, citar o termo “malandragem carioca” e ter dificuldade em administrar o tempo.

articles.title: Local de votação: veja como consultar mudanças para o 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Justiça Eleitoral mudou pelo menos 554 seções entre o 1º e 2º turno. Tribunal orienta que eleitores chequem o local de votação no dia da eleição, antes de saírem de casa.
articles.summary: Confira como consultar o local de votação pelo e-Título ou site do TSE após a Justiça Eleitoral confirmar mudanças em centenas de seções para o 2º turno.
articles.body:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) informou, na sexta-feira da semana passada (16), a mudança nos locais de votação neste 2º turno das eleições. Segundo o TSE, até o momento, 554 seções eleitorais no Brasil tiveram alterações entre o primeiro e o segundo turno. Em 25 de outubro, serão decididos o presidente da República e os governadores de cinco estados e do Distrito Federal.

O TSE orienta os eleitores a conferirem o local de votação pelos canais oficiais do tribunal . A consulta pode ser feita pelo aplicativo e-Título ou pelo menu Autoatendimento Eleitoral , no portal do tribunal ( veja o passo a passo abaixo ). Segundo o TSE, eventuais mudanças de endereço ainda podem ocorrer até a data da votação, mas apenas "em último caso".

Veja abaixo como consultar o seu local de votação nas plataformas oficiais da Justiça Eleitoral.

Disponível gratuitamente nos celulares Android e iOS, o aplicativo da Justiça Eleitoral pode ser usado como identificação na hora da votação e também mostra os dados atualizados sobre o local de votação.

Para acessar as informações, baixe o aplicativo, acesse a ferramenta com os dados solicitados e selecione a opção "Onde Votar". Lá, você pode conferir a zona e a seção eleitoral.

O aplicativo e-Título, da Justiça Eleitoral, possui todos os dados atualizados sobre o eleitor, o local de votação, entre outros serviços. — Foto: Reprodução

Pelo app também é possível justificar a ausência no dia da eleição e realizar o descadastramento como mesário voluntário, entre outras funções.

Autoatendimento Eleitoral nos sites da Justiça Eleitoral

A ferramenta está disponível nos sites do TSE e dos TREs (Tribunal Regional Eleitoral) dos estados e permite consultar informações, regularizar pendências, atualizar dados e emitir documentos de forma remota. Para acessá-la, entre no site e clique na aba "Autoatendimento Eleitoral" .

Depois, vá até a opção "Consultas" e clique em "Onde votar". Preencha os campos com os seus dados pessoais (número do título, CPF ou nome; data de nascimento e nome da mãe) e clique em "Entrar".

A partir disso, será possível checar todas as informações sobre o título: regularidade, local de votação, endereço e localização por meio do Google Maps.

O Autoatendimento Eleitoral permite a consulta do local de votação nos sites do TSE e dos TREs pelo país — Foto: Reprodução

A ferramenta é um assistente virtual da Justiça Eleitoral, que utiliza inteligência artificial para responder dúvidas e orientar os eleitores. Para acessá-lo, entre no site do TSE e localize o ícone no canto inferior direito da tela. Clique sobre o ícone e digite a sua dúvida.

O ChatVote, ferramenta de IA da Justiça Eleitoral para tirar dúvidas dos eleitores. — Foto: Reprodução

Cartórios eleitorais e atendimento telefônico

Caso esteja sem internet ou não possa acessar as informações remotamente, o eleitor pode comparecer ao cartório eleitoral mais próximo para verificar os dados atualizados.

Também é possível entrar em contato, por telefone, no Disque Eleitoral de cada Tribunal Regional Eleitoral. Entre no site do TRE do seu estado e veja qual é o número oficial.

Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, eventuais mudanças no local de votação acontecem por motivos práticos, desde "reformas de última hora e melhorias de acessibilidade em prédios públicos até o impacto de fortes chuvas".

Na sexta (16), o TSE havia anunciado a mudança de 4,3 mil seções eleitorais. O número, no entanto, se revelou bem menor, já que a página da Justiça Eleitoral havia contabilizado como alteração no local de votação os casos em que, na prática, alguns endereços das seções se mantiveram entre o 1º e o 2º turno. Depois, o dado foi corrigido e será atualizado até o domingo.

As divergências também foram identificadas pelos TREs dos estados, que estão divulgando em seus sites e redes sociais quais locais de votação realmente mudaram. O TSE reforçou que as alterações não são decididas de forma centralizada, e que a responsabilidade cabe a cada zona eleitoral, que avalia a infraestrutura disponível para a eleição.

O g1 apurou, até o momento, alterações em pelo menos nove estados. Confira abaixo, em cada estado, quais são as seções eleitorais que sofreram mudanças.

articles.title: Accountability is coming: Trump aides face looming congressional probes
articles.summary: As the midterms approach, Congressional investigators are prepared to probe allegations of corruption and misconduct involving President Trump’s appointees and close associates.
articles.body:
The constant stream of crazy news stories coming out of the Trump administration is a bowl full of distractions, until a glance under the chaos reveals crass corruption.

Sixty percent of voters now rank “government corruption,” as their top concern, according to a Fox News poll released last week . Corruption is a bigger issue than inflation or gas prices, with the midterm elections just days away. Exposure of the corruption will go beyond Election Day.

Congressional investigators will soon be asking how a Trump ambassador with access to national security information was revealed to have sent a “Honey Please,” demand for money to a Trump donor.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece, resigned after reports that she allegedly solicited $100,000 from the businessman to pay her personal credit card bill ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, according to The Wall Street Journal .

Any ambassador with undisclosed financial obligations, as well as reported ties to dealmakers looking to profit from American investments overseas, is vulnerable to blackmail and extortion.

Congressional investigators, Republican or Democrat, might also ask how a former TV host and former girlfriend to the president’s son, with no diplomatic experience, became an ambassador.

Government prosecutors have largely failed to hold Trump accountable for multiple charges of misconduct .

But as Trump’s time in office expires, the people around him responsible for reckless and self-serving actions cannot assume they will have the same power to stay out of jail.

There will be a particularly hot congressional spotlight on several aides now representing Trump overseas. Did they mix the nation’s global affairs and even the use of the American military with their personal business?

That list of high-flying Trump associates includes Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. They have been largely free of scrutiny as the president’s top foreign policy negotiators. But with Trump’s hold on Congress fading in his last years in office, Witkoff and Kushner face increasing odds of being called for congressional testimony.

They will have to handle questions about their talks about billion-dollar oil refinery deals that “would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties…” to Witkoff and Kushner, according to reporting in last week’s New York Times.

Also likely to have to testify under oath before Congress are the president’s sons, Eric and Donald Trump Jr.

Both are heavily involved in cryptocurrency ventures, promoting an industry that has become a favored instrument for people skirting taxes and international sanctions law on business deals. Crypto is also a haven for hiding funds used by drug traffickers, and kidnappers. With Trump in office, his family has made billions from crypto .

Corporations have privately given Trump hundreds of millions for his ballroom project while several have government contracts, The Washington Post reported last week.

A former Trump aide likely to sit before Congress is the former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia. In her week on the job Zacharia stumbled in handling questions about her background and work in China. On television, she has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But journalists uncovered that she never practiced law in the U.S. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that she took the California bar exam and failed.

When reporters asked where she passed the bar, she offered an answer referring to her move to China. But foreign nationals cannot simply take the Chinese bar examination and become licensed Chinese lawyers. And her husband was involved with major business deals in China while she worked at a law firm in China.

Was that history uncovered in security-vetting process done by the White House?

Failure to properly report professional credentials and foreign ties is grounds for questioning. The government can’t function with officials who can’t be trusted with sensitive government information.

Last year, Joe Cirincione, a national security analyst, described the people Trump was nominating as ambassadors as “a diplomatic clown car that’s about to be rolling up at the Capitol with all these idiots. … Where’s the outrage?” The outrage is now likely to emerge in congressional hearings.

Furious questioning is in store for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Another former television personality with no government experience, Hegseth has overseen American military strikes that killed people in the Caribbean. Videos of the attacks were released by Hegseth’s team at the Pentagon. The administration described the targets as drug smugglers and made a spectacle of their deaths. But the evidence for using lethal U.S. military force against these alleged traffickers has never faced investigation by prosecutors or serious congressional scrutiny.

That was before Hegseth proposed showing the nation a livestreamed firing-squad execution of a man in a wheelchair . The White House later called off the barbaric display.

Using their subpoena power, congressional investigators need to prime the pump on reviewing financial disclosures, security-clearance applications and quid-pro-quo deals. They need to probe wasteful government contracts and the misuse of military force. Review of the financial dealings of presidential relatives and associates is overdue.

The records exist. The witnesses exist. Congress has the power to uncover the truth.

And the objective should be accountability, not political revenge. Polls show Americans, Republicans and Democrats, see the corruption. Accountability is coming. The diplomatic clown car is long overdue to be pulled over by police and the vehicle searched from tip-to-tail.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.summary: The Supreme Court rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew. The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006. Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial. The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences. But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal. Military courts said he had no such authority but, in an August ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in favor of the government, prompting the men to appeal to the Supreme Court. They argued, among other things, that the appeals court had no authority to intervene in the case. The long delay in Mohammed facing trial was caused partly by concerns about evidence obtained via CIA torture. A fourth alleged plotter earmarked for trial, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, was not involved in the appeal.

articles.title: Supreme Court to decide if 160-year-old home distilling ban is constitutional
articles.summary: The Supreme Court said Monday it will consider whether the government can ban people from distilling spirits at home, after a lower panel declared restrictions dating to the 1860s unconstitutional. The Trump administration urged the justices to get involved, saying the lower court took a “blinkered view” and its decision threatens the viability of longstanding…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court said Monday it will consider whether the government can ban people from distilling spirits at home, after a lower panel declared restrictions dating to the 1860s unconstitutional.

The Trump administration urged the justices to get involved, saying the lower court took a “blinkered view” and its decision threatens the viability of longstanding federal taxes on producing vodka, whiskey and other distilled spirits.

“The government has a substantial interest in its authority to safeguard a significant source of tax revenue—a source that was used to pay Revolutionary War debts at the Founding and now generates billions of dollars in tax revenue every year,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the administration’s petition.

The case is set to be heard this term. Oral arguments are likely to be held early next year, with a decision expected by summer.

First enacted in the 1860s, federal law makes it a felony to produce distilled spirits “in any dwelling house” or in a connected “shed, yard, or inclosure.” Violations can carry up to five years in prison.

In defending the law, the government ties it to federal excise taxes on distilled spirits as old as the country’s founding. They were a significant revenue source for the new government, even provoking the famed Whiskey Rebellion as citizens violently protested the new duties.

Congress can enact measures that are “necessary and proper” to exercise its constitutional powers — like taxation — but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit rejected that the ban falls within that power.

Sauer says the law makes it more difficult for distillers to conceal their operations and avoid taxes.

“Those practical realities have not changed. Today, as at the time of enactment, a distiller can more easily conceal a distilling operation (or conceal a spirit’s strength and avoid the proper tax rate) if a still is located at a dwelling-house or another business,” he wrote.

The law faces a challenge from the Hobby Distillers Association and four individuals who want to distill spirits at their homes.

Despite having won, a separate appeals court hearing a different lawsuit reached a conflicting result, so the association agreed the Supreme Court should settle the issue.

“Homebrewing revitalized beer culture in the United States; home distilling could do the same for spirits, but for the prohibition,” they wrote in court filings.

articles.title: High spirits: Supreme Court to decide fate of federal ban on home distilling
articles.summary: The Supreme Court announced it will consider whether to strike down a longstanding federal ban on distilling spirits at home.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — In a boost for those who want to make whiskey in their bathtubs or gin in their kitchens, the Supreme Court on Monday announced it will consider whether to strike down a long-standing federal ban on distilling spirits at home. Although interest in the home distilling of hooch has continued despite the 150-year old ban, advocates hope the court will remove the threat of criminal sanctions, which can include a fine of up to $10,000 and a maximum sentence of five years in prison. For decades, people have been able to make wine and beer at home for personal use without any penalties. The distilling ban was enacted in 1868 in a bid to counter tax evasion by those making spirits. It bars the distilling of spirits in “any dwelling house” or surrounding structures. The challengers include the Hobby Distillers Association and several of its members. One, Scott McNutt, has a still at home that he has used to distill fuel alcohol. Another, Rick Morris, owns a company that manufactures stills that can be used at home. They sued in Texas after being told by the federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, part of the Treasury Department, that they could not obtain a license to distill at home because of the federal ban. The lawsuit contains several claims, including that Congress exceeded its taxing power by passing a ban that did not actually raise any revenue. In a separate challenge brought in Ohio, another would-be home distiller, John Ream, raised similar claims. The two cases resulted in conflicting rulings by federal appeals courts. In the Texas case, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals backed the challengers, while in the Ohio case, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion. As a result, both losing parties appealed, and all parties agreed the Supreme Court should issue a definitive ruling that would apply nationwide. If the challengers win, they would still have to register their stills and pay excise tax on the spirits they produce, even though it would be for their own consumption. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, representing the federal government, defended the law in court papers, saying that it is within the power of Congress to restrict taxable activities by location if there is a strong chance the taxes will not be paid. Similar to marijuana, which remains broadly illegal under federal law while various states have legalized it, several states allow home distilling, including West Virginia, which legalized it in 2024. Those laws do not take precedence over the federal ban. Legislation has also been introduced in Congress to repeal the federal restrictions.

articles.title: Supreme Court turns away appeal from 9/11 defendants seeking to reinstate plea deals
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear appeals from three men accused of plotting the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks who are currently awaiting trial at the infamous Guantánamo Bay prison. The justices turned away petitions from Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, without explanation. Justice Brett…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear appeals from three men accused of plotting the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks who are currently awaiting trial at the infamous Guantánamo Bay prison.

The justices turned away petitions from Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, without explanation.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from the Mohammed and al-Hawsawi petition.

The three prisoners were seeking to reinstate plea deals in which they agreed to plead guilty and give detailed confessions about their roles in the deadliest terrorist attack in U.S. history. In exchange, prosecutors would not have sought the death penalty.

A Pentagon official approved the deals in late July 2024, but then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin nullified them two days later following criticism from some victims’ families.

A military judge ruled that Austin’s attempted withdrawal had come too late because the defendants had already “begun performance.” A unanimous panel of military appellate judges upheld that decision.

A divided panel for the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the decision the following July, finding that Austin had acted within his legal authority when he backed out of the deals.

In separate petitions, the defendants argued that the appellate court was not authorized to hear the government’s challenge. Bin Attash also argued that it was wrong of the appeals court to conclude that he had not begun fulfilling his obligations under the agreement because he had already signed a stipulation admitting to the basis for the charges.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer had urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeals, arguing that it would ensure the decision of whether to pursue the death penalty is made by an “official who answers to the American people.”

“The court of appeals correctly exercised jurisdiction to reject the military judge’s extraordinary disregard for the Secretary’s authority over these military-commission prosecutions of paramount national significance,” Sauer wrote.

The three men were charged jointly for allegedly helping plan and orchestrate the 9/11 attacks more than two decades ago. Nearly 3,000 people were killed when members of the al Qaeda terrorist group hijacked four commercial planes, crashing them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pa.

They are set to be tried together in a military trial scheduled to begin in early June 2028. The start date has been pushed back several times.

articles.title: Americans saying US on ‘wrong track’ hits record high for second Trump term: Poll
articles.summary: A majority of Americans in a new survey believe the U.S. is on the “wrong track” as the midterms approach, marking a record high during President Trump’s second term. The NBC News Decision Desk poll, using data from SurveyMonkey, found that 71 percent of respondents said the country is heading down the “wrong track.” The…
articles.body:
A majority of Americans in a new survey believe the U.S. is on the “ wrong track ” as the midterms approach, marking a record high during President Trump’s second term.

The NBC News Decision Desk poll , using data from SurveyMonkey, found that 71 percent of respondents said the country is heading down the “wrong track.” The poll marks the first time that the “right track” response fell below 30 percent since Trump returned to the White House — with 29 percent saying the U.S. is on the “right track.”

The state of the economy also weighs on many Americans as the issue that matters most, according to 31 percent of respondents and 35 percent of independents. Eighteen percent said their financial situation is better off today than it was last year, but 44 percent say it is worse now and 38 percent say it’s about the same as it was last year.

Another issue on respondents’ minds is gas prices , with 67 percent saying the higher costs tied to the ongoing Iran war are “very serious” or “somewhat serious,” compared with 33 percent who said the price hike is “not too serious of a problem” or “not a problem at all.”

Respondents also see government corruption as a major issue plaguing the country, with 56 percent saying the concern is equal between both parties. About 25 percent said it’s a bigger issue in the Republican Party, and 17 percent say it’s worse in the Democratic Party, the survey found.

This thinking carries over to the Trump administration, where 52 percent of respondents see it as “more corrupt” than previous administrations, while 25 percent said it is less corrupt. Roughly 23 percent said the administration is just as corrupt as its predecessors, according to the data.

About 52 percent of respondents say Democrats should start impeachment proceedings against Trump if they win control of the House in November, as 48 percent say they should not.

Americans also say they don’t buy Trump’s pledge to give every adult $5,000 if Republicans keep their control of Congress, with 71 percent saying they “definitely” or “probably” do not expect to receive a check if the GOP maintains its majorities. Another 14 percent say they “definitely” or “probably” expect those checks to go out.

Polling has frequently shown Democrats likely reclaiming the House and possibly even the Senate after the November midterms, opening the likelihood of firm legislative opposition during Trump’s final two years in the White House.

The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ shows a 77 percent probability that Democrats win back the House, with a narrow 56 percent probability of claiming the Senate.

The NBC Decision Desk survey was conducted Sept. 28 to Oct. 12 and included 19,135 respondents with a margin of error of 2.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Supreme Court to hear a new case on race and school admissions, this time in Maryland
articles.summary: The Supreme Court agreed to hear a new challenge to school admissions policies on diversity, taking up a case on magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a new challenge to school admissions policies aimed at fostering diversity, taking up a case targeting a lottery-based process for magnet programs in a Maryland county. The court agreed to take up an appeal brought by the Association for Education Fairness seeking to revive a lawsuit it filed against the Montgomery County Board of Education. Montgomery County is a large and diverse county in the suburbs of Washington, D.C. The challengers argue that a policy in Montgomery County's STEM and humanities magnet schools unfairly elevates Black and Latino students for admission in violation of the 14th Amendment. In 2023, the Supreme Court cited the same amendment in striking down the use of race in college admissions. But this case is narrower, asking the justices to decide a more technical question of what evidence challengers need to bring such a claim, so the court is not poised to issue a ruling on the constitutional issue. The policy in question concerns a group of four middle schools with magnet programs. The current programs are entered via lottery, a system introduced during the Covid pandemic. Entry to the lottery is based on how well students perform on tests when ranked against others in their school, which the plaintiffs say adversely affects Asian students in high-performing schools. The challengers have targeted that process, as well as one first introduced in 2017 (which has been discontinued) that sought to increase enrollment of children in low-poverty areas. That program, sparked by a report that said Black and Latino students were underrepresented and Asian students overrepresented in the middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County schools, included outreach to students and a cognitive test. The plaintiffs say both programs were explicitly aimed at increasing Black and Latino enrollment, thereby violating the Constitution’s 14th Amendment. Since the court’s 2023 decision, conservatives, including members of the court, have accused colleges and schools of trying to circumvent the ruling by introducing new admissions policies that have the same purpose but do not explicitly consider race as a factor. Similar cases reached the court, but the justices declined to take them up. A federal judge in Maryland and the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals both ruled in favor of the school district. It’s the second time in recent years the court has heard a case challenging policies in Montgomery County Public Schools. Last year, the court ruled in favor of parents who objected on religious grounds to LGBTQ-themed books approved for use in elementary school classrooms.

articles.title: Betting on the election? Your state may prohibit it
articles.summary: The midterm elections are fast-approaching, but can you wager on them?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – With the expansion of online betting platforms, you can wager on nearly anything, from the Super Bowl to who will be selected as the White House press secretary (suspicious bets tied to the latter are being investigated ).

Politics has seemingly become one of the most popular spaces in which wagers are being cast. Earlier this year, for example, Kalshi banned former Rep. George Santos after he placed wagers on the State of the Union.

Prediction markets, in particular, have been a focus of lawmakers for several months. In March, bipartisan legislation was introduced in the Senate to restrict what entities like Kalshi and Polymarket can offer wagers on .

Several states are also targeting prediction markets and even warning voters against betting on their ballots.

In July, election officials in Wisconsin warned voters that betting on an election could not only cost them their vote but culminate in a felony charge.

“We want voters to understand that they cannot legally make a bet on an election and cast a ballot in that same election,” Wisconsin Election Commission Administrator Meagan Wolfe said. “We are not able to police someone placing a bet on these platforms, but it’s important for voters to understand the consequences if they bet on an election outcome.”

Wisconsin is one of several states that prohibit election betting, at least in some circumstances, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Others like it include Oregon, North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Indiana, New York, and Massachusetts.

Twenty-four other states – Idaho, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas, Iowa, Arkansas, Louisiana, Illinois, Michigan, Tennessee, Mississippi, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, West Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island – have blanket prohibitions on election betting, NCSL reports.

Texas has been weighing how prediction markets could impact elections . In August, the issue was discussed during a Texas House Elections Committee hearing on emerging election technologies, according to Nexstar’s KXAN.

The state prohibits gambling on election outcomes, as well as political nominations and appointments. However, prediction markets argue they offer swaps or exchanges, not traditional betting, exempting them from the rule.

Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ, called prediction market betting in the 2026 midterm elections “ the Wild West right now .”

“We’re in real new territory, and it’ll be interesting to see how state and federal governments and others respond to it,” he told The Hill.

States without prohibitions on betting on elections, according to the NCSL, are Alaska, Hawaii, California, Washington, Montana, Wyoming, New Mexico, Kansas, Missouri, Ohio, Kentucky, Virginia, Alabama, Florida, Connecticut, Maine, Vermont, and New Hampshire.

Sixty percent of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released this week said they did not support betting on election results.

articles.title: Why California’s Racial Justice Act isn’t just enough just yet
articles.summary: The Golden State’s approach to racial bias in the courts has been widely praised. Sadly, a series of court decisions have weakened its protections.
articles.body:
In 2020, the state of California took a dramatic and important step to address persistent racial inequities in its criminal justice system by enacting the Racial Justice Act. It followed Kentucky and North Carolina in passing a law specifically targeting the pervasive problem of racial discrimination in the criminal justice system.

Such legislation was a response to a 1987 Supreme Court decision limiting the use of statistical evidence to prove racial discrimination in capital sentencing. The court held that a defendant must “prove that the decisionmakers in his case acted with discriminatory purpose,” and offer evidence “specific to his own case that would support an inference that racial considerations played a part in his sentence.”

But as the Stanford Center for Racial Justice reports, “Defendants are rarely successful in meeting that standard.”

Enter California’s Racial Justice Act, which expanded the means by which defendants “can show discrimination,” allowing them to “establish racial bias by relying on statistical data showing racial disparities in the charging, conviction, or sentencing process of other defendants who share their race.”

The law makes it illegal for the state to “seek or obtain a criminal conviction or seek, obtain, or impose a sentence on the basis of race, ethnicity, or national origin.” It targets “racially discriminatory language about the defendant’s race, ethnicity, or national origin” and cases where a “defendant was charged or convicted of a more serious offense than defendants of other races who have engaged in similar conduct.” Finally, it prohibits sentences that are “longer or more severe” in one case than in “other similarly situated individuals convicted of the same offense.”

Where violations occur, the Racial Justice Act requires courts to do things like vacating convictions or sentences, and ordering new proceedings consistent with the act. And if race played any role in a capital case, it forbids prosecutors from seeking the death penalty.

The Racial Justice Act went a long way toward sweeping away other barriers and technicalities that have often prevented courts from remedying racial discrimination in criminal cases. One example is the so-called “harmless error” rule that tolerates errors “not damaging enough to the appealing party’s right to a fair trial to justify reversing the judgment.” The Racial Justice Act makes it clear that when it comes to race, no errors are harmless. That signals something important about the ambition of California’s law.

The Golden State’s approach has been widely praised. The Public Policy Institute of California, for instance, says it “goes beyond any other state or federal attempt to ensure equal treatment under the law for all races.”

However, in August, the state supreme court severely weakened the law in the case People v. Hazlett by excluding “racially discriminatory use of peremptory challenges” of jurors from the protections that the Racial Justice Act affords criminal defendants.

Justice Kelli Evans dissented from this decision, calling its reasoning “cramped.” “When a prosecutor strikes a juror based on a discriminatory belief,” she wrote, “this is necessarily bias ‘towards the defendant because of the defendant’s race.’”

In September, we saw another consequence of the court’s cramped interpretation of the act in the case of Monte Haney . In that case, the California Court of Appeals dismissed a claim of racial discrimination in jury selection, citing the reasoning behind Hazlett.

Judge Jon Streeter, while concurring, took the occasion to argue that “Racial Justice Act’s objective is to eradicate all forms of racial bias in any criminal proceeding in the California courts at every stage from the beginning to the end. … Time will tell,” he continued, “whether, in the view of the Legislature … Hazlett is consistent with the level of judicial commitment to uprooting racial bias in criminal cases that the Legislature has repeatedly stated in legislative findings it wants to see in the application of the [Racial Justice Act].”

While judges can and do debate the meaning of statutory language and the intent of its authors, the last word lies with the legislature. It has already shown itself willing to improve the Racial Justice Act and extend its reach. Four years ago, in 2022, the legislature amended the act to make it retroactive and afford relief to people convicted and sentenced before the law was enacted.

In 2025, reacting to a series of court decisions that “eviscerated” the law, the California legislature observed that, “Like a metastatic cancer, racial bias in one part of a criminal prosecution infects the whole and cannot be remedied by removing a single diseased cell. Remedies must match the gravity of the ills of racial bias and not be so narrow as to minimize the harm or fail to address it in its entirety.”

California law already prohibits “using peremptory challenges to remove jurors (in cases involving a civil rights violation and civil commitment of a person) based on race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, national origin, or religious affiliation.” Now, the legislature has another chance to ensure that the Racial Justice Act applies to bias in jury selection in criminal cases. When it does, it will again make California’s commitment to eradicating racial bias in criminal cases a model for the nation.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Johnson says he warned White House of ‘unintended consequences’ from Russia sanctions waiver
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that he warned the White House of “unintended consequences” that could stem from waiving sanctions on Russia. President Trump signed an executive order last week waiving sanctions on Russia that were slated to take effect under a legislative package championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and passed by…
articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that he warned the White House of “unintended consequences” that could stem from waiving sanctions on Russia .

President Trump signed an executive order last week waiving sanctions on Russia that were slated to take effect under a legislative package championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support. The move quickly sparked bipartisan backlash.

Asked whether he wants to waive the tariffs or forgo the move, Johnson told Fox News host Larry Kudlow, “Congress voted on this decisively just several weeks ago, and we understand that Putin cannot be trusted.”

“He demonstrates that over and over and over,” Johnson said. “So I did talk to several of my colleagues yesterday who had concerns about that. They’re on committees of jurisdiction, like intelligence and foreign affairs, and I didn’t talk to the president yesterday because he and I are both traveling nonstop and we’re on different schedules. But I told the White House team that we need to talk about it, and I think carefully consider the unintended consequences that may ensue from that.”

Johnson added that he knows the “president’s evaluating this as he does everything else.”

“Look, he has two major objectives, as you know, Larry. Every day he wants to keep America safe, and he wants to bring down the cost of living for every American. He thinks outside the box with creative ideas all the time, and he carefully evaluates those. So I think the right decision will be made here in the end,” Johnson said.

Several GOP lawmakers, meanwhile, were quick to bash Trump’s move.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote on the social platform X.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on X that the president is “prolonging the war, not ending it.”

Trump has defended the move, writing in a Truth Social post that he is “in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

articles.title: Now that Musk owns Republicans, they own his extremism
articles.summary: Why is Musk exempt from the kind of scrutiny devoted to social media influencers who have far less influence on our culture and political system?
articles.body:
Elon Musk, whose “ world’s richest man ” status relies heavily on money his companies get from U.S. taxpayers , is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to try to keep Republicans in control of Congress. He has spent more than $275 million in just the past few months, on top of the more than $100 million or so he had already spent this election cycle.

I sure would like to see more reporters asking Republican candidates to disavow Musk for promoting racist and inflammatory rhetoric; or for turning X into a platform that empowers neo-Nazis and white supremacists; or for amplifying anti-immigrant rhetoric to a point that led to mob violence; or for pushing, in the words of The Nation’s Jeet Heer, “global neo-Nazi regime change.”

Why is Musk exempt from the kind of scrutiny devoted to social media influencers who have far less influence on our culture and political system?

Earlier this year, the Guardian reported that many of Musk’s X posts were “indiscernible from those of white supremacists.” For example, Musk reposted a claim that “white genocide is the official Democrat party platform.” This spring, the Washington Post quoted a commentator noting that Musk’s “near daily” posting about race left “no doubt he’s a white nationalist.”

Musk has repeatedly endorsed the idea of “ remigration ” — the idea that non-white immigrants should be forced to leave the U.S. and European countries. He promoted the movie “Citizen Vigilante,” and the idea that violence should be waged against “first the traitors, then the invaders.” And he has called anyone who opposes remigration a “traitor.”

When a journalist told him it was irresponsible to promote a movie that “glorifies the murdering of a Muslim immigrant family,” Musk insisted that it is “worth watching.”

As New York Times writer Jamelle Bouie has asked , “Why do we tolerate Elon Musk’s racist commentary?” And why are we letting Republicans get away with relying on Musk’s millions to save their seats without demanding some accountability for their partnership?

It’s easy to understand why Republicans themselves are silent in the face of Musk’s extremism. It’s not just because they’re depending on Daddy Warbucks to save their skins from a voter revolt. And it’s not just because they don’t want to anger Trump while the president is honoring Musk and putting more of our national security infrastructure in his hands.

The disturbing but undeniable truth is that most Republican officials in the age of Trump have either fully embraced or chosen to tolerate the kind of inflammatory race-baiting and anti-immigrant rhetoric Musk and Trump spew to their millions of social media followers.

Republicans cheered as Musk gleefully fed the U.S. Agency for International Development into the woodchipper and made life more miserable for millions of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable people, potentially leading to hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Republicans’ reaction to Musk is akin to their largely going silent about the epic, historically unprecedented levels of corruption that have seen Trump’s personal and family wealth skyrocket through billions in shady self-enriching deals.

Speaking of self-enrichment, the over quarter of a billion dollars Musk spent in the 2024 elections to put Trump back in power turned out to be a fantastic investment for his own pocketbook. Investors’ anticipation of the billions in no-bid contracts that would come his way was enough to boost Musk’s wealth by $50 billion in the week after the election. His net worth had grown by 69 percent before Trump even took office. Since then, both of them have seen their wealth soar.

And the Department of Justice dropped ongoing investigations into Musk’s companies. Just a little thank you.

No objections from congressional Republicans. They have gone along for the ride as the Justice Department has been turned into a vehicle for Trump’s revenge fantasies. Its Civil Rights Division has abandoned its historic mission and embraced the right-wing fiction that white Christian men are the most persecuted people in our country.

Meanwhile, Christians who do experience real persecution in many parts of the world are denied the opportunity to find refuge in the U.S., because just about the only people the Trump administration is willing to accept as refugees are white South Africans. It is a policy that reflects South African native Musk’s influence and widely disputed claims of “white genocide.”

In short, Musk is MAGA at its worst. At a time when voters are souring on the corruption and cruelty of Trumpism, Republican candidates should be held accountable for their silence.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.title: National Guard member shot in DC after trying to break up fight
articles.summary: A member of the National Guard was shot in the leg late Sunday while attempting to break up a fight in Southeast Washington, police said Monday. The injured guard member and the suspected shooter were hospitalized, and their injuries were not deemed life-threatening. The shooting occurred around 11:10 p.m. EDT in the 400 block of…
articles.body:
A member of the National Guard was shot in the leg late Sunday while attempting to break up a fight in Southeast Washington, police said Monday.

The injured guard member and the suspected shooter were hospitalized, and their injuries were not deemed life-threatening.

The shooting occurred around 11:10 p.m. EDT in the 400 block of 8th Street SE, according to interim Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) Chief Jeffery Carroll. Seven or eight National Guard members were “monitoring” a group of people gathered on a sidewalk.

A fight broke out and troops exited their vehicles to try to intervene, when they “heard gunshots” as they approached the group, Carroll noted during an early morning news conference.

One of the suspects involved in the altercation had opened fire, prompting guard members to order the person to drop their weapon, according to police.

“That individual then pointed the weapon toward National Guard members, who returned fire,” the police chief said.

Three guard members fired their weapons, shooting the suspected gunman in the abdomen. One guard member was also shot in the leg during the confrontation.

Carroll said it was not immediately clear which member fired the shot that struck the suspected gunman, whose identity has not been released.

MPD’s Internal Affairs Division and Criminal Investigation Division are investigating the shooting. Carroll said there were “no further threats to the community.”

The shooting comes nearly a year after two National Guard members were shot and injured blocks away from the White House, leaving one dead and another critically wounded.

The soldiers were first deployed to the nation’s capital to help tackle crime last year. Their stay was extended earlier this year through the 2029 presidential inauguration.

articles.title: Former Trump aide: Prospect of replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller ‘terrifying’
articles.summary: Sarah Matthews, a former White House deputy press secretary, said Sunday that the prospect of President Trump replacing chief of staff Susie Wiles with deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller was “terrifying” amid speculation Wiles will depart after the midterms. Trump has dismissed reporting that Wiles could soon leave her post, but Matthews told MeidasTouch’s…
articles.body:
Sarah Matthews, a former White House deputy press secretary, said Sunday that the prospect of President Trump replacing chief of staff Susie Wiles with deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller was “terrifying” amid speculation Wiles will depart after the midterms .

Trump has dismissed reporting that Wiles could soon leave her post , but Matthews told MeidasTouch’s Jack Cocchiarella that Trump “is unhappy with the way things are right now” and appears to be blaming Wiles.

“He’s been doing his favorite thing, which is calling around, seeing what people think of different names that he floats if he chooses to replace her,” Matthews said. “Publicly, he said that he’s sticking with Susie, but we know that he’s making these calls, and one of those names is Stephen Miller.”

“And that is a terrifying prospect,” she added.

Matthews said Wiles is not “crazy” but accused her of being “complicit in the horrors of this administration.”

“Stephen Miller is bats— crazy,” she continued. “And the idea that in the last two years of Trump’s administration, when he’s going to be spiraling because he’s a lame-duck president … The idea of someone like a Stephen Miller in charge is a very scary thing.”

Matthews told Cocchiarella that she and Miller “interacted here and there,” including when Matthews would work with former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany before briefings during Trump’s first term. She said Miller would go to McEnany’s office and “help consult if we felt like we needed his guidance on something or advice or whatever it was.”

Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney told NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” that he expects Wiles to depart the White House after the midterms “not necessarily because she’s fallen out of favor with Trump. It’s just a natural sort of time to make that change.”

Trump said Politico’s reporting Thursday about Wiles departing in the near future was “TOTAL FAKE NEWS,” accusing the outlet of not caring about “facts, integrity, or honest journalism –– it’s why I kicked them out of the White House!”

“Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that,” he said in a statement. “She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”

Trump told CNN on Friday that Wiles has “been incredible” and will be with the White House “for a long time.”

Wiles is seen as one of Trump’s most trusted advisers and confidants, shaping his second administration after serving as his 2024 co-campaign manager.

Following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year, Trump praised Wiles as an “amazing person” and an “amazing fighter.” She said in September she was cancer free .

articles.title: Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen in California sweep targeting alleged noncitizen voters
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who o...
articles.body:
Election 2026 California Noncitizen Voting

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered or voted in U.S. elections.

The arrests are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month's midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare , difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Federal officials on Monday blamed California officials for the alleged crimes, accusing them of facilitating noncitizen voting through inadequate voter roll maintenance and hiding it from the public. The charges escalated a simmering voter roll fight that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued California and warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution.

The Justice Department said the 28 people who were charged as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations.

"This causes real damage to real elections and real damage to American citizens," Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department, said during a news conference in Los Angeles.

Rob Bonta, California's Democratic attorney general, said Monday that there is no widespread voter fraud in California and that while "one-off" examples of voter fraud are possible, those instances are "a drop in the bucket" considering the state has 23 million registered voters.

Bonta said he expects his state to prevail in the federal government's lawsuit, saying the Republican administration "has provided us with no facts of any ineligible voters, just a conclusory statement with no evidence to back it."

California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute

The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. While some states voluntarily handed over the information, the department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain it — lawsuits that so far have been unsuccessful .

The Justice Department said Monday it has charged 113 people in 20 states with illegal voting and illegal registration offenses over the last seven weeks. It earlier said it had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens . There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.

The operation Monday involved the four U.S. attorneys' offices across California in what the Justice Department intended as a statewide show of force.

Among the dozens of people arrested was a 72-year-old Belize-born man who is accused of voting illegally in four elections.

Dozens of federal agents descended on Omar Alexander Muñoz's residential cul-de-sac in Commerce, a small city in Los Angeles County, to make the arrest. Muñoz was put in handcuffs in his pajamas and taken into federal custody downtown.

Esmeralda Muñoz, 70, said her family was furious that agents showed up to their home in full tactical gear with guns drawn to arrest her husband before dawn.

"It's a show for them," she said, calling it a "shame" that government officials arrived with camera crews and news helicopters.

She and her three children and 10 grandchildren are all U.S. citizens, she said; Omar Muñoz is a legal permanent resident, she said, and they didn't realize that he was registered to vote. When they do talk about politics, Esmeralda said Omar has been a vociferous supporter of Trump.

The arrests were the latest in a flurry of activity that has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.

The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.

The complaint was filed after California officials were given , and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.

McCotter said the 20,000 number was likely to rise.

DOJ accuses California of 'state-facilitated voter fraud'

McCotter said the lawsuit against California was necessary because "state-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable," and accused state officials of creating the last-minute emergency before Election Day by not working with the Justice Department sooner to check alleged noncitizen voters.

Explaining why it was important to address voting by noncitizens even though it's rare, he noted that some races in California have been decided by just hundreds of votes.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, criticized the state's election officials for not cooperating with the department's demands.

"Why is California refusing to show their voter rolls?" he asked. "What are they afraid of? What are they hiding?"

As part of its lawsuit, the Justice Department filed paperwork Monday seeking a court order that would force California to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens and to independently, or in conjunction with the federal government, verify their citizenship status before tabulating their mail-in ballots. The Justice Department asked for the order to be entered in time for the Nov. 3 election.

Absent that order, the government said, "there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted."

Requests for comment sent Monday to the secretary of state and governor's office were not immediately returned. Governor Gavin Newsom on Monday published a series of X posts seeking to undermine the Justice Department's announcement.

"WOW. First Assistant Bill just admitted in front of the press that not all of those arrested today may have voted," he wrote in one post, referencing Essayli.

On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation.

A letter from McCotter reads: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.

In response, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away.

"The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court," he said.

Associated Press writers Eric Tucker in Washington, Ali Swenson in New York and Sophie Austin in Sacramento, California, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Supreme Court takes up new case over race and school admissions
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will hear a challenge to admissions policies at a suburban Maryland county’s competitive middle school, the justices announced Monday. It’s a key test of the court’s 2023 decision invalidating affirmative action in higher education admissions. That decision left open questions over what lengths school districts may still take to promote diversity. An association of Asian…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court will hear a challenge to admissions policies at a suburban Maryland county’s competitive middle school, the justices announced Monday.

It’s a key test of the court’s 2023 decision invalidating affirmative action in higher education admissions .

That decision left open questions over what lengths school districts may still take to promote diversity.

An association of Asian American parents wants to revive a challenge to Montgomery County’s new admissions policy, launched in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, to select students for the district’s magnet middle school programs that focus on STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — and the humanities.

The county still screens students based on their grades and test scores. But at a second stage of the process, the county conducts a lottery to determine which students get a seat at the magnet school.

The group, called the Association for Education Fairness, says the policy violates the Constitution’s Equal Protection guarantee. Lower courts dismissed the claims.

The association says courts used the wrong legal standard and wants the justices to provide a nationwide resolution for what evidence a plaintiff must show to invalidate a racially neutral policy as discriminatory.

“Yet the governing constitutional standard now depends on geography,” the group’s lawyers wrote. “Evidence sufficient to establish an Equal Protection claim in some circuits is legally irrelevant in others.”

The case is set to be heard this term. Oral arguments are likely to be held next year, with a decision expected by summer.

“The Constitution protects students as individuals, not as members of a racial group,” said Chris Kieser, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation, a libertarian group that represents the parents. “A school district should not be able to defeat a discrimination claim by showing that its policy did not harm enough Asian American children. Every family deserves admissions rules that judge their child on their own merit.”

Montgomery County’s school board told the Supreme Court the case is “unremarkable and of little significance” and is not the best way to sort out the proper evidentiary standards.

“This case involves a race-neutral lottery adopted in response to a global pandemic. It is not the right fact pattern for this Court to take up the question presented,” the board’s lawyers wrote.

The high court agreed to get involved after receiving multiple similar appeals from other areas in the wake of the affirmative action decision.

In 2024, the court turned away a challenge to a revamped admissions policy at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, one of the nation’s top-ranked high schools, located in the Virginia suburbs of the nation’s capital.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, both members of the court’s conservative wing, had publicly indicated they wanted to take up the case.

“The Court’s willingness to swallow the aberrant decision below is hard to understand,” Alito wrote at the time.

Months later, the duo similarly dissented as the court declined to get involved in the battle over admissions practices at Boston’s prestigious “exam schools.”
