articles.title: Warren warns against Sysco-Restaurant Depot merger
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) on Sunday warned against a merger between Sysco and Restaurant Depot, arguing it could lead to an increase in restaurant prices. “Watch out: going out to eat at your favorite restaurant could become even more expensive,” Warren wrote on the social platform X. “The Trump administration might approve a merger…
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) on Sunday warned against a merger between Sysco and Restaurant Depot, arguing it could lead to an increase in restaurant prices .

“Watch out: going out to eat at your favorite restaurant could become even more expensive,” Warren wrote on the social platform X . “The Trump administration might approve a merger between Sysco and Restaurant Depot — threatening higher supply costs for small businesses and higher prices for you.”

Warren is the top Democrat on the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, and she is in line to chair the panel next year if her party takes control of the upper chamber in November.

Sysco, a multinational food distributor, agreed in March to purchase Restaurant Depot, which supplies food to independent operators.

Under the $29.1 billion deal, Restaurant Depot shareholders will receive $21.6 billion in cash proceeds and 91.5 million Sysco shares. The two companies anticipate closing by the third quarter of fiscal 2027.

Officials from the two companies said in March that the deal would give the combined entity access to Sysco’s higher-volume customers, which include restaurants, healthcare and educational facilities and sports stadiums, and Restaurant Depot’s independent restaurants and businesses.

Under federal law, the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) review mergers for antitrust concerns. The Hill has reached out to the department and the FTC for comment on the review of the Sysco-Restaurant Depot merger.

Restaurant Depot would operate as a standalone business within Sysco. Kevin Hourican, the CEO of Sysco, has also insisted his company will not raise Restaurant Depot’s prices upon closing the deal.

“It would harm the Restaurant Depot business if we did that,” he said in an August release , referencing raising prices. “We would lose share if we did that.”

Hourican added there “was no economic incentive” to raising prices.

Prices for food away from home, as measured by the consumer price index, increased by 0.2 percent from August to September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported last week.

The price of food away from home was up 3.5 percent year-over-year last month, while annual inflation for food at home was 1.8 percent, according to the BLS.

articles.title: Trump takes border crackdown to deep-red state as shock Senate battle threatens GOP stronghold
articles.summary: Donald Trump heads to Kansas to rally near Wichita, touting his immigration agenda as ICE arrests and deportation efforts ramp up across the state.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: WICHITA, KANSAS — President Donald Trump is expected to tout his immigration agenda in ruby-red Kansas on Monday, weeks after federal immigration agents made dozens of arrests in the southwestern portion of the state. Trump is headed to the Sunflower State for a rally just outside of Wichita as a tighter-than-expected Senate race that could determine the balance of power in the upper chamber unfolds. Fox News Digital has learned that Trump will lean into the policy positions that helped propel him and Republicans to power two years ago. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER "President Trump stopped the invasion of our country and delivered Americans the most secure border in American history," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Under the President’s leadership, 3 million illegals have left the United States and zero illegals have been released at the border in seventeen months." "Meanwhile, radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies, abolish ICE, and grant amnesty to the illegal aliens they released into our communities," she continued. The Trump-led Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have touted a string of arrests and deportations of illegal immigrants in the state over the last several months. GEORGIA ICE SWEEP NABS OVER 700 CRIMINAL ILLEGAL ALIENS, INCLUDING SEX OFFENDERS, CHILD ABUSERS According to the White House, among some of the "worst of the worst" who were arrested in the state by federal immigration officers include Omar Israel Hernandez of Mexico, convicted of first-degree murder, Jose Luis Rauda-Diaz of El Salvador, convicted of aggravated robbery and two counts of possession of a weapon, Oscar Sanchez-Corona of Mexico, who had previously been deported for drug offenses, damaging property, and driving under the influence, Greg Chukwuka Orji of Nigeria, convicted of dangerous drugs and possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, and Alberto Estrada of Mexico, convicted of aggravated indecent liberties with a child and rape. Trump’s rally comes as the race between Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton has cranked up in a state the president has won by double-digits in the last three presidential cycles and has given Republicans cause for concern in a state where voters haven’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan race ranker, downgraded the contest to a toss-up earlier this month and money from GOP and Democratic groups is flowing into the state. KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ Marshall, who is vying for a second term, has run close to Trump, rarely breaking from him on key issues throughout this cycle. Hamilton, however, has run away from the Democratic establishment in Washington, D.C., and warned that if elected, he wouldn’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term leading the caucus. Trump’s appearance in the state also follows ICE’s three-day sweep in Southwest Kansas last month, dubbed "Operation Safe Community — Kansas," where agents made over 100 arrests. Marshall pushed back on the operation, demanding that "when ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement." "Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe," Marshall said on X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, Republicans have targeted Hamilton for his immigration stance, accusing him through ads run by outside groups, like the Senate Leadership Fund, of supporting mass amnesty. Hamilton, however, pushed back on the Biden administration’s immigration policies and told the Johnson County Post that the previous administration's open border policies "caused a different kind of chaos." "Record crossings overwhelmed communities, and the immigration courts fell years behind," Hamilton said. "I’m not for open borders, and dangerous criminals don’t belong here."

articles.title: When history reckons with Donald Trump, it won’t forget America’s role
articles.summary: Someday each of us will be asked the question, “What did you do when people were killed on the streets?”
articles.body:
Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, recently told the National Catholic Reporter that we are going through “ a dark night of the soul as a country .”

Just last month, several children gathered in a courtroom to have their futures decided by a Texas judge. One was a six-year-old who pretended to fly an airplane; another was a three-year-old who played with a microphone. They were among 25 minors facing deportation hearings that day.

Angel was one of them. Just 13 years old, he pleaded that it was “too dangerous” to be returned to Honduras, adding, “My mom and my entire family are here.” The judge ruled that Angel did not qualify for asylum and asked whether he wanted either a deportation order or would leave voluntarily. At that, Angel burst into tears crying : “I have no one. I have nothing.”

The stories of those young Texas children are not the only examples of the cruelties inflicted upon immigrants by the Trump administration.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have murdered U.S. citizens and patrol our streets. Children wonder whether their parents will be home when they return from school. And many immigrants who have followed the rules are being deported not to their home countries, but to places like South Sudan, Eswatini and Rwanda .

Earlier this year , Renée Good and Alex Pretti became household names when they were publicly executed on the streets of Minneapolis. In Biddeford, Maine, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a food delivery worker, was killed by an ICE officer in front of his wife and three-year-old daughter. Houston, Texas, saw Lorenzo Salgado Araujo gunned down by ICE agents as he was on his way to a job at a construction site.

During the past year, 37 people have died in ICE custody, many with Hispanic surnames whose identities are not household names but are known to God.

At a Catholic mass held for the World Day of Migrants and Refugees, Washington, D.C., Cardinal Robert McElroy recited the story of the Good Samaritan. In it, Jesus Christ describes a priest and Levite who saw a robbery victim laying on the side of the road and passed by. Only the Samaritan stopped, treated the victim’s wounds, and paid for his stay at a nearby inn.

As Cardinal McElroy noted , it’s easy to dislike the priest and the Levite, and admire the Good Samaritan.

When migrants are deported, raids on farm workers and Home Depots take place and mothers and children are detained, many of us have assumed the role of the priest and Levite and passed on by.

When the Trump administration dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which has saved millions of lives overseas, many wondered, “What can we do?”

Donald Trump has called himself “ the greatest president ever .” Scholars disagree. Steven Levitsky, a professor of government at Harvard University, contends that during Trump’s second term in office the U.S. has “slid into some form of authoritarianism.”

Americans are equally disenchanted with Trump. An Economist/YouGov poll finds hefty majorities describe him as “arrogant,” “opportunistic,” “reckless,” “dishonest,” “corrupt,” “hypocritical” and “divisive.”

It is easy to characterize the past decade as the era of Trumpism, a word that encompasses the cruelties inflicted by Trump, the degradation of our political institutions and attacks on the rule of law.

Using a word to describe a political era happened once before during the 1950s, when Sen. Joseph McCarthy (R-Wisc.) charged that the U.S. government had been infiltrated by communist sympathizers. Harry Truman declared that McCarthy’s only importance was that his name “has taken on a dictionary meaning”.

“It is the rise to power of the demagogue who lives on untruth; it is the spreading of fear and destruction of faith in every level of our society.”

Truman’s definition of McCarthyism can be applied to the word Trumpism. But the danger is that like the 1950s, we will look upon this present moment and blame one man who used his power for nefarious purposes. Someday each of us will be asked the question, “What did you do when people were killed on the streets, or children held in detention, or when other cruelties too numerous to mention were inflicted on others?”

Did you, as Cardinal McElroy said, “ pass on by ”? Or will you be able to say that you protested, voted or otherwise made your views known?

In his 1953 inaugural address , Dwight D. Eisenhower offered “a little private prayer” to the Almighty: “Give us, we pray, the power to discern clearly right from wrong, and allow all our words and actions to be governed thereby, and by the laws of this land.”

He asked for cooperation to be the goal for those who “hold to differing political faiths; so that all may work for the good of our beloved country and Thy Glory.”

This too, should be our prayer. A historical reckoning with Trump is coming.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics. “

articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Sunday that President Trump had “stuck a shiv in the back” of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) legacy following his decision to waive Russian sanctions included in legislation named after the senator. The board accused Trump of being “best friend in the world” to Russian President Vladimir…
articles.body:
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Sunday that President Trump had “stuck a shiv in the back” of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) legacy following his decision to waive Russian sanctions included in legislation named after the senator.

The board accused Trump of being “ best friend in the world ” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, adding that “the evidence compounds that Mr. Trump wants Ukraine to surrender on Mr. Putin’s terms.”

“When the election is over there needs to be a bipartisan reckoning for Mr. Trump’s budding alliance with the Kremlin against Ukraine, Europe and American interests,” the editorial board concluded in its piece.

Trump waived the sanctions in the legislative package , which was posthumously dedicated to Graham, that was intended to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its years-long military operations against Ukraine. The legislation imposed tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and those who help the country evade sanctions.

The president defended the decision to do so, writing on Truth Social that his administration was “in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine” and didn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

“Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want,” he continued.

The move drew bipartisan ire as the legislative package passed the House and Senate with wide margins ; Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) even called the waiver “entirely irresponsible.”

“The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media, referring to Friday’s order.

Other GOP lawmakers have been critical of Trump’s proximity to Putin and the Kremlin in recent days following the president’s Russian oil deal amid rising global energy prices.

Under the agreement , the president said Russia could “immediately” begin supplying 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November and then 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky slammed both of Trump’s decisions as the waiver marked another flashpoint in the world leaders’ relationship.

On Sunday, Zelensky stated in an interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” that Ukraine trusted Trump , adding that it would be “unbelievable” for the U.S. to support Putin over him.

articles.title: Khanna blames wealth inequality, not immigration, for youth protests in Europe
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Sunday blamed wealth inequality, not immigration from the “global south,” as the reason behind the youth protests igniting across Europe, including in France. “From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an…
articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Sunday blamed wealth inequality, not immigration from the “global south,” as the reason behind the youth protests igniting across Europe, including in France .

“From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in,” Khanna wrote on the social platform X .

Khanna said French students and teachers are taking to the streets “asking for safe schools, enough teachers and smaller classes.”

“In Spain, for affordable rent and housing,” he continued. “In Albania, for good jobs and an end to corruption.”

He took a swipe at Vice President Vance, who on Saturday accused “western liberals” who “imported the third world … in the name of diversity and compassion” while ignoring “fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

“@JDVance says this is what happens when a nation lets in too many immigrants from the global south,” Khanna wrote. “He is not just morally wrong, but misreading the moment. The is what happens when nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few. This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future.”

Khanna called on Americans to “listen to our young” and said the U.S. needs “an economic and political transformation.”

“America’s Next New Deal,” he concluded, referring to former President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s transformative economic policies enacted in the years after the Great Depression hit in 1929.

President Trump has also made the unfounded claim that the protests are because of “ out of control mass migration ” and “Islam wanting to take over a once great Country.” Trump and Vance echoed other conservatives who blame the European Union’s immigration policies for the protests.

Hundreds of thousands of French protesters, including union members and student organizations, took to the streets in marches against the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools. Some demonstrations across France turned violent as protesters clashed with police and businesses faced fires and looting.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Saturday accused the protesters of being “extremely violent, radical far-left groups” who are targeting city halls and local government offices, The Associated Press reported.

Nearly 2,400 people have been arrested in connection with Saturday’s protests, with nearly 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, including seven who were severely hurt, Nuñez said.

Nuñez told Time magazine on Monday that police “lost control” of some cities over the weekend and that there was a “lack of anticipation” prior to the start of demonstrations on Saturday. He said he offered his resignation to French President Emmanuel Macron, saying he “felt responsible” for the protests spreading.

Macron refused his resignation because of “the need for a continuous command of the police, the Élysée Palace told the outlet. The president on Sunday condemned what he called in a televised speech “unbridled violence,” Le Monde reported .

articles.title: Trump’s midterm message to his base: It’s an American Golden Age, just not for you.
articles.summary: In an opinion piece, Joslin Joseph argues that Donald Trump’s administration prioritizes corporate and wealthy interests during its current economic era while leaving his core supporters to bear the financial burdens.
articles.body:
A con man will look you straight in the face and tell you his con with a straight face. As President Trump jet-sets on a non-stop tour to prevent the midterm bloodbath that pundits are predicting, he isn’t just going to battleground states. His stops in very heavily red states have turned heads as his trademark chaos strategy has people wondering if he can mitigate the impending massacre.

Is he trying to encourage MAGA voters to turn out in large numbers? Is he just on an ego trip to deal with the dismal poll numbers? Is he trying to create content that shows large crowds that can be played in battleground states to portray that people still rabidly support him? Or are the numbers on the ground in heavily red states just that bad too? It might be a combination of all and we probably won’t find out until after Election Day, but Trump’s midterm message to his base has been consistent and brutally honest.

This is an American Golden Age, just not for you. This is the best it has ever been in America, but you have to pay the price. People are making money hand over fist, but you, my base, have to go through pain in order for this gravy train to be maintained. While campaigning in Arizona, Trump proclaimed that “ we’re making a fortune ” on oil prices. Most Americans reacted like Uncle Phil in “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” when Will Smith’s character said, “we’re rich.”

But this was Trump being his most honest. He has lied about everything from elections to inflation to his golf game. But in this midterm push, he has finally revealed what the plan was the whole time. The people he cares about are making money. His family is raking it in , billionaires are getting richer so that they can blow over $150 million on a Texas Senate campaign, corporations are reporting record profits while laying off workers , and fraudsters are paying for pardons . People who can pay to access the president and his family, are living their best life.

Trump’s base? They are paying the price, both literally and figuratively, for Trump’s Golden Age. Food pantries in West Virginia can’t keep up with demand for food relief. Diesel prices have hurt farmers (among others) where their costs have increased by thousands of dollars a week. States hurt most by gas prices are primarily red. His base is paying and for what? A feeling that they owned the libs?

There are two universal truths of the American voter. The first is that Americans vote with their wallets. The second is that Americans will compare themselves to others. The Republicans have usually been amazing using the latter truth to get votes. They will go to voters and say, “Things are tough on you, but look at those illegal immigrants getting free things.” Or they will say, “You are just getting by but look at those welfare queens gaming the system.” They may ask, “Why are people on welfare buying lobster and getting the latest iPhone?” They might also say, “Your kid might not have gotten good grades, but their spot at a top-notch university was taken by a Black kid because of DEI.”

It works because life is hard and when you perceive others getting a break, you get resentful. Trump voters often will say they turned to him because they felt they were left behind. They were right, for the most part. Trump’s populism gave them the hope he would enrich them but would also ensure those they were told were unjustly reaping the benefits would no longer be able to.

And here we are. You can’t blame illegal immigrants, DEI, welfare recipients, Black Americans, woke liberals, universities, medical experts, or even the Democrats anymore. Trump voters gave him everything so he could improve their lives. Yeah, they got to feel patriotic and like they were winning a game whether it was political, religious, cultural, or all of the above against the rest of us, but at some point, their lives should have improved.

Think about every president in your lifetime. Has any one of them told you that in order for this country to be great, that you had to suffer? They might have said times were tough for everyone, or that we as a country were about to go through some challenges, but no president has ever trotted out to his most ardent supporters and told them this is the best it has ever been, just not for you.

Trump voters now have to buy a literal “check in the mail” promise and hope that at some point the wealth will flow downward toward them. Because of the Big Beautiful Bill, tariffs, and war with Iran along with a president set on enriching people that he cares about, they might have to wait a very long time. At some point, you have to realize if you aren’t already coming out on top in this “Golden Age,” you have been conned.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: How a foreign government helped accused Saudi spy's family flee US after OpenAI bug scandal
articles.summary: A former OpenAI engineer was in frequent contact with Saudi royalty and searching company records on the Kingdom before his arrest, prosecutors say.
articles.body: A former OpenAI engineer accused of secretly planting listening devices inside the artificial intelligence giant's facilities was communicating with Saudi royalty and searching company records involving the Kingdom before his arrest, according to federal prosecutors who are investigating whether his alleged surveillance was intended to benefit a foreign government. In a detention filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Saudi government officials helped arrange international travel for Abdulrahman Alfozan's wife and three-month-old son shortly after his arrest. They also raised concerns about Alfozan's potential access to foreign government assistance if released. Prosecutors disclosed that Alfozan had been in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi royal family who sought to recruit him for a Saudi artificial intelligence initiative. The filing does not allege that Saudi Arabia directed his alleged surveillance. TRUMP INTEL CHIEF WARNS AI FIRMS ON HACKS, SAYS NEW DEPARTMENT IS THE 'COP ON THE BEAT' The investigation remains ongoing and "may result in additional serious charges," prosecutors said. Investigators are examining whether Alfozan sought to record sensitive OpenAI meetings to advance his own business interests, aid a foreign government or both. According to the filing, Alfozan spent weeks researching how to construct an encrypted recording device with live-listening capabilities and where inside OpenAI he could capture sensitive conversations. He allegedly used an internal OpenAI tool to identify meeting rooms used by company executives and outside partners before concealing a customized audio recorder behind a television in an executive conference room in late September. The room regularly hosted leadership meetings, technical and product discussions, and briefings with government officials and business partners. Conversations frequently involved proprietary research, OpenAI's technical capabilities, strategic decisions, government engagements and commercial relationships, according to prosecutors. Government officials met with OpenAI executives in the room around the time of the alleged surveillance, prosecutors said, warning that Alfozan's conduct "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." Investigators also uncovered evidence suggesting his alleged surveillance extended beyond a single device. OpenAI security personnel discovered a second similar recorder inside a bag Alfozan left in a printer room. Searches of his home and electronic devices subsequently uncovered similar components and photographs that appeared to show reconnaissance of other locations inside OpenAI, including another conference room used for sensitive meetings. Investigators say Alfozan was also showing particular interest in OpenAI's dealings with Saudi Arabia. His browsing history showed that he accessed a folder titled "Saudi Gov Docs" on Oct. 4, 2026, and used an internal OpenAI tool to search for engagements involving Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. Among the subjects he searched were planned OpenAI visits to Saudi Arabia, an upcoming visit by the Saudi ministry and a meeting labeled "HUMAIN x MCIT @OpenAI," according to prosecutors. At the same time, Alfozan maintained frequent contact with an unidentified member of the Saudi royal family, including just four days before his arrest. "Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!" the royal told Alfozan in May, according to the filing. Alfozan responded "100," which prosecutors interpreted as agreement. The royal repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan for an artificial intelligence initiative in Saudi Arabia and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI. Alfozan said he would not leave until his stock vested, according to prosecutors. He was also allegedly pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including applying to the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation's "2030 Leaders" program. GOOGLE ENGINEER STOLE AI SECRETS FOR CHINA, SENATE HEARS IN EXPLOSIVE TESTIMONY The Saudi connections have become a focus of prosecutors' argument that Alfozan poses a serious flight risk. At the time of his arrest, Alfozan had one-way tickets from San Francisco to Riyadh for Oct. 12, 2026, and was scheduled to begin two months of parental leave from OpenAI. The FBI arrested him Oct. 9, 2026. The accused's wife and infant son initially had a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia booked and paid for by the Saudi government, prosecutors said. Then a Saudi military official purchased business-class tickets for the pair en route to Qatar. They departed San Francisco roughly 36 hours after Alfozan's arrest. Prosecutors cited the travel arrangements as evidence that Alfozan could receive substantial assistance from the Saudi government if released. Fox News Digital has reached out to the Saudi Embassy, OpenAI and Alfozan's attorney for comment. The government also pointed to a previous federal case in which prosecutors alleged that a former Twitter employee received Saudi assistance leaving the United States after being confronted over his access to internal user data. After Twitter confronted employee Ali Alzabarah in 2015, prosecutors alleged, calls were exchanged with a Saudi foreign official and the Saudi consul general in Los Angeles to coordinate a flight to Saudi Arabia the following day. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Alzabarah later went to work for the Misk Foundation, according to the filing. Charges against him remain pending. Prosecutors argued that Alfozan similarly has access to "considerable support from a foreign government" with no extradition treaty with the United States and the resources to provide extraordinary travel assistance. Alfozan, a legal permanent resident, was earning $385,000 annually at OpenAI and had received a $2.2 million equity grant, according to prosecutors. OpenAI fired him following his arrest. He is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. Prosecutors are asking a federal judge to keep him behind bars pending trial, arguing that he poses a serious flight risk and an ongoing danger to the community.

articles.title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
articles.summary: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.
articles.body:
Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".

The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.

US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.

Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.

Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.

"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.

"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.

"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."

Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.

In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.

Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".

But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".

Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.

Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

articles.title: The fifth Musketeer wields the wealth of nations
articles.summary: In place of a sword, Musk is armed with nearly a trillion dollars.
articles.body:
Alexandre Dumas’s “ The Three Musketeers ” were swashbuckling novels taking place in 17th century France. Athos, Porthos and Aramis, with the young d’Artagnan — great name for a small dog — sword fight their way against the villainous Cardinal Richelieu with the great refrain, “one for all and all for one.”

Today there is a fifth and perhaps greater Musk-eteer — Elon.

In place of a sword, Musk is armed with nearly a trillion dollars . If Musk were a country, he would rank 23rd in total GDP . That wealth makes him the second and perhaps even the most powerful man in America, possibly eclipsing the president. Consider why.

In the coming November elections, Musk will spend close to a half billion dollars in support of Republican candidates, far more than all other leading contributors. Assuming some win, that gives Musk even greater political clout and influence. He is a frequent guest at the White House, recently decorated by President Donald Trump with some award for something.

Second, Musk is the only person — including President Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin — who can end the war in Ukraine on his terms. Last week, Musk withheld use of Starlink’s Starshield , crippling Ukraine’s ability to command and control its forces and especially drones. And Ukraine may not have a workaround to fill this potentially fatal flaw.

Imagine then how Musk could coerce President Volodymyr Zelensky into accepting a Carthaginian or draconian peace favorable to Moscow. Trump has more than signaled aiding Moscow by purchasing millions of gallons of Russian diesel fuel. The proceeds most likely will not go to propping up Russia’s failing economy. Instead, the dollars will be used to finance the war against Kyiv. Ending Starlink would be the coup de grâce.

Third, how powerful could Musk be in international affairs? Consider the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia . With the stroke of a pen and the transfer of a few billions, might Musk be able to achieve in Saudi Arabia what the U.S. government has failed in Iran — regime change?

Most do not realize that Mohammed bin Salman is sitting on a political power keg. In late 2017 and early 2018, bin Salman arrested and held hostage nearly 400 of Saudi Arabia’s wealthiest families in Riyadh’s Ritz Carlton. Most were released after paying huge amounts of what was ransom money. But that unleashed a tsunami of resentment that still persists.

While bin Salman controls the security apparatus, if the Houthis continue attacking vital Saudi infrastructure such as the attack that closed down King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, this is an assault on the regime. With Musk money, the Houthis could expand these attacks further weakening bin Salman’s hold on the country.

As the United Kingdom and the U.S. overthrew Iran’s Prime Minister Mohammed Mossadegh in 1953, provoking eternal hostility, surely Musk is capable of that in Saudi Arabia — or at least has the money if he is so inclined. That does not mean it will happen. Collateral damage will affect the extended Trump family as son-in-law Jared Kushner’s venture fund is backed by bin Salman. But it is possible.

Suspend reality for a moment and consider 2028. Suppose Musk was to run for president. While the Constitution forbids non-native born Americans from election, with tongue in cheek, Musk could say he was born in the USA — the Union of South Africa.

But what would prevent him from being vice president? In the event the president died or became incapacitated, the next in succession would be the Speaker of the House of Representatives, given Musk’s constitutional ineligibility. And what candidate of either party would not want him as a running mate given the $5 or $10 billion he could throw into the race?

Few if any Americans have ever wielded as much power as the president. Only John Pierpont Morgan comes to mind bailing out the country in the financial panics of 1895 and 1907. Not even the great Robber Barons John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie possessed the wealth and clout of Morgan and now Musk.

With Tesla, SpaceX and any future ventures he may have planned, Musk is one of the world’s most powerful people. Suppose as a further thought experiment, China’s President Xi Jinping or Putin proposed an alliance with Musk. That would transform international politics and possibly end the Westphalian system of state-based politics because Musk is a man who does not need a state as a power base.

Or suppose Musk buys a small country? The possibilities are endless. And, in this case, the Fifth Musketeer rides alone, in which one for all and all is for him.

Harlan Ullman (X: @harlankullman) is chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos.”

articles.title: Elissa Slotkin wants to scare, threaten young Republicans away from politics
articles.summary: This is not how politics should work in a free country that holds democratic elections.
articles.body:
Elissa Slotkin is a Democratic senator from Michigan, and supposedly one of the more moderate members of her party. But even Slotkin wants to use the power of the federal government — power she hopes to wield if Democrats take back the Senate — to punish her political opponents.

In recent remarks of hers that went viral, Slotkin brags about wanting to discourage young Republicans from getting involved in politics and joining the Trump administration by making them fear the threat of prosecution. Take a look.

That footage came courtesy of The Chicago Thinker, an independent paper at the University of Chicago, where Slotkin spoke last week. And did you get all that? She’s talking deterrence: She wants young Republicans to fear that they will face legal consequences for getting involved in government. That’s what she wants to do with the congressional majority: wage lawfare against Republicans and members of the administration so totally and completely that no one will even want to work for President Trump, because they can’t risk it.

That’s pretty awful. It’s an attitude of absolute moral superiority of certainty Slotkin possesses that her side is right about everything and thus justified in effectively cheating at politics. She wants to rig the system. She wants to punish people who disagree with her. Is that what we’re coming to? As that the vision the Democrats have for the country? Why not prosecute people if they break the law, not simply because we don’t like them and want them to suffer in hopes it sends a message to others?

And keep in mind, Slotkin is supposedly a moderate. When far-left Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America get into Congress, their reign of terror will be even further reaching. It will be even more illiberal. It will be aimed at making it difficult or impossible to dissent from their agenda.

This is not how politics should work in a free country that holds democratic elections. We don’t want to be the sort of nation where everybody goes to jail when there’s a turnover election. But the Democrats continue to push things in this direction. Unfortunately it’s going to get much worse.

So let’s take them at their word. A Democratic victory in the midterm elections, a Senate majority in addition to a House majority, will mean they’re coming after everybody. That’s their theory of deterrence, and their plan to make it so that the federal government is even more ineffective than it was previously: drive young people who disagree with them away from politics forever. Brace yourself, lawfare is coming.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Hatch Act complaint filed against Carr, Burgum and Lutnick
articles.summary: Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders filed a Hatch Act complaint against three Trump administration officials for campaigning in Alaska with Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) earlier this month. The complaint asks the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate appearances and brief remarks delivered at Sullivan’s rally by Federal Communication Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan…
articles.body:
Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders filed a Hatch Act complaint against three Trump administration officials for campaigning in Alaska with Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) earlier this month.

The complaint asks the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate appearances and brief remarks delivered at Sullivan’s rally by Federal Communication Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that allegedly violated the Hatch Act.

The Hatch Act bans federal employees from taking part in political activities while on duty or on federal property.

“Although FCC Chairman Carr explained that he was speaking in a personal capacity, his short remarks were focused on past and pending work of the FCC,” the complaint read. “At no point did either Secretary [Burgum or Lutnick] … remark that they were speaking in their personal capacity.”

The complaint also alleges President Trump introduced Burgum and Lutnick by their official titles. Since they failed to “correct the impression that each was speaking officially,” they “appear to have used their official positions while engaged in political activity,” which is in direct violation of the Hatch Act.

The complaint noted that the FCC has an upcoming vote on an Alaskan broadband deal, which Carr discussed the day after the rally, writing on social platform X , “I look forward to working with @SenDanSullivan to get the job done.”

While Trump unveiled a $4.4 billion investment into an Alaskan pipeline project from Taiwan at the rally, he credited Sullivan during the rally for helping him “get this done.”

“In referring to their official work, these agency heads leaned on their official roles to support their political activity,” the complaint continued.

Clayton Weimers, the executive director of Reporters Without Borders North America, stated in a press release that Carr, particularly, had “annihilated any sense of independence the FCC once had.”

The U.S. Office of Special Counsel stated on its website that penalties for Hatch Act violations included removal from federal service, debarment from federal employment for a period not to exceed five years, suspension, reprimand or a maximum civil penalty of $1,000.

When asked about the complaint, a Department of Interior spokesperson told The Hill, “This is an absurd attempt by a leftist group, that is led by an Obama era political appointee, to push baseless claims.”

“Secretary Burgum attended in his personal capacity which is in full compliance with DOJ guidance and the Hatch Act,” the spokesperson continued.

The FCC and Commerce Department did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

The U.S. Office of Special Counsel confirmed it received the complaint but declined to comment further.

articles.title: Trump’s golf course showdown tees off in DC
articles.summary: Plus: 😒 GOP backlash over Russia grows {beacon} It’s Monday. New week, fresh start and another chance to convince ourselves we’ve got it all together. In today’s issue: DC golf course plans hit resistance GOP backlash over Russia grows Affordability concerns hinder Trump message Hegseth’s future on the line Programming note: Hello!…
articles.body:
It’s Monday. New week, fresh start and another chance to convince ourselves we’ve got it all together.

Affordability concerns hinder Trump message

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Elliott Davis filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to sthomas@thehill.com or edavis@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Julia Demaree Nikhinson and Mark Schiefelbein

President Trump has big plans for one of Washington, D.C.’s most popular public golf courses. But first, he’ll have to get past a federal judge who isn’t backing down on her scrutiny of the project amid mounting questions about its legality.

All eyes are on Monday’s hearing over the future of East Potomac Park, where U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes is pressing the administration for answers after crews cut down hundreds of trees earlier this month, including some of the park’s famous cherry trees.

Courtroom showdown: Reyes refused the Justice Department of Justice’s (DOJ) demand that she step aside over accusations of bias. Trump piled on Monday , calling her a “crazed lunatic” in a post on Truth Social.

Now, the judge wants to hear directly from officials who actually know Trump’s plans for the property — testimony the DOJ has so far resisted. And she’s prepared to keep the hearing going all day if that’s what it takes.

What’s Trump planning? The president unveiled a proposal Sunday to turn the affordable public course into a championship-level facility designed by famed architect Tom Fazio , with hopes of hosting major professional tournaments.

The president says the course will close Nov. 15 for a renovation lasting roughly 15 months.

But local golfers and preservationists aren’t exactly cheering. They’re worried about the future of the popular recreational space, while questions remain about the project’s cost and environmental impact.

The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo breaks it all down in Keeping Score. 📖 Insiders can read here .

Trump is facing growing frustration from within his own party over Russia — and with the midterms just two weeks away, the timing isn’t ideal.

Republicans are pushing back against the president’s decision to waive sanctions against Moscow, just days before they were set to take effect under a law Congress passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.

Sens. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Darline Graham (R-S.C.) have pushed back on the move, while Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) argued the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — whose name is on the sanctions law — would be appalled.

Trump and his administration are defending the pause, arguing that keeping the economic pressure off the table could help encourage Russia to enter into talks to bring an end to its war with Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also lambasted the U.S. over Trump’s efforts to broker an energy ceasefire. Both sides have also launched fresh strikes on the other in recent days.

The backlash goes beyond sanctions relief: Four Republican senators also joined with Democrats last week in demanding a Pentagon watchdog investigation into possible restrictions on intelligence sharing and satellite internet services for Ukraine. The reported Starshield slowdown is raising questions about whether Pentagon officials acted without Trump’s knowledge or approval.

The big question: Can lawmakers actually force the president’s hand? That’s far from certain, even as the president faces continued backlash over the separate diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin .

And with Election Day fast approaching, the growing rift is creating another political headache for Republicans as Trump hits the campaign trail.

Trump heads to Kansas on Monday as Republicans face a tricky closing stretch with his foreign policy decisions threatening to complicate their midterm pitch.

The president is looking to boost Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in the competitive Senate race against Democrat Adam Hamilton, but his moves abroad are becoming campaign issues back home.

The Hill/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) polling average puts Hamilton at 46.6 percent support and Marshall at 46.1 percent. The visit follows recent campaign stops in Georgia, Arizona and Montana.

In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson recently broke with Trump over the diesel deal. Meanwhile, the war with Iran has pushed energy prices higher, putting more pressure on Republicans already struggling to sell voters on the economy.

The DDHQ’s average has Trump’s approval rating sitting at 39.9 percent, with 58.6 percent disapproving. Democrats also hold a nearly 8-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot.

The question now is whether Trump’s campaign stops can help Republicans steer the conversation back to their own priorities.

Libertarian candidates could shake up tight Senate races in Texas, Kansas and Iowa.

They’re currently polling in the low single digits, but that could be enough to make a difference. And with control of the upper chamber of Congress at stake, every vote counts.

👓 Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky .

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may have another fight on his hands after the midterms — this time over his own job.

Senate Democrats are quietly floating his removal as part of a deal to move stalled defense legislation , The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports. And they may find some willing partners across the aisle.

Several Republicans have grown frustrated with Hegseth’s leadership, while Democrats are threatening to block defense funding and efforts to fill key Pentagon vacancies, including a waiver for acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to take on the role full time.

The sticking point: Trump remains firmly behind Hegseth, and some Republicans doubt he’d agree to push him out just to get a deal done. But with defense funding expiring Dec. 11 and impeachment efforts potentially returning after Election Day, the pressure is building.

Plus, Hegseth’s Pentagon departure list is getting long.

Dan Driscoll : Army secretary, resigned in August.

Randy George : Army chief of staff, forced into retirement in April.

John Phelan : Navy secretary, pushed out in April.

Christopher Donahue : Top Army commander in Europe, retired early in June.

🗳️ As the midterms approach, outside groups are working to secure the election results amid concerns that the Trump administration could interfere in the process to keep Republicans in power. The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch and Mike Lillis have more for Insiders here .

🏠 In the face of backlash against the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), White House border czar Tom Homan maintained in a Sunday Fox News interview on Fox News that investigators have “strong evidence” against the Minnesota lawmaker.

🐘 Let the (way-too-early?) blame game begin: The knives are already out among Republicans as Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton faces negative headlines and lagging polling numbers against Democrat James Talarico .

🏫 Early childhood educators are worried that changes proposed by the Trump administration, including some that would impact Head Start, could hurt their working conditions as teachers already deal with staffing shortages and low pay.

🏛️The Supreme Court is set to consider whether the government can ban people from distilling spirits at home — restrictions that date back to the 1860s. The justices will also take up a Maryland school admissions case involving allegations of racial discrimination, while declining to revive 9/11 plea deals .

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington and Kansas. (All times EDT)

articles.title: No Kings account suspended by Meta during protests — not a coincidence?
articles.summary: Whether we’re talking about Brazil or the United States, the issue is bigger than one Instagram account or one algorithm. It’s about transparency, accountability and whether the digital platforms shaping political conversations are applying their rules fairly.
articles.body:
One group organized nearly 3,000 events over the weekend with tens of thousands of attendees and one big goal: getting voters ready for next month’s midterms.

“No Kings” mobilized across the country, helping people check their voter registration, understand their voting rights and make a plan to cast their ballots. But in the middle of that nationwide push, the movement says its main Instagram account was suspended at a critical moment.

According to Newsweek, the account was down for roughly 90 minutes , and organizers say they remained locked out of the account’s administrative tools for hours afterward, so they couldn’t post, completely limiting their ability to communicate with supporters.

Meta apologized, saying the suspension happened by mistake after an automated system flagged the account’s high volume of activity.

But organizer Ezra Levin isn’t convinced this is simply a story about a computer making a mistake.

“This is strikingly reminiscent of what we saw in Brazil.” he said. “Just this week, a court ruled against Meta for favoring the authoritarians in that country and we might be seeing something similar from Meta in our country right now.”

So, for context, Brazil is heading into an Oct. 25 presidential runoff between left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, of unfairly restricting its political content while giving Bolsonaro’s campaign an advantage. One concern involved Meta’s AI tools.

A Brazilian nonprofit named CTRL + Z reported over 1,000 cases of reduced visibility, account bans, or electoral censorship disproportionately affecting pro-Lula content. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court ordered Meta to ensure equal treatment of the candidates across its platforms. The court upheld that order unanimously, with a hefty fine for violations.

In the Brazil incident, Meta again denied intentional political bias and pointed to technical issues and its election-related safeguards. That’s a very convenient response for a private company that controls platforms that millions of people rely on for political information.

The whole point of the No Kings movement is showing that President Trump’s second administration has concentrated too much power in the presidency, undermining democratic norms. Its organizers are now trying to turn that opposition into votes.

“No Kings” may sound like a dramatic title, but Trump is has behaved in a way that exhibits unchecked executive overreach. A new Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that 66 percent of Americans say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself . Whether it’s ignoring the emoluments clause, dissolving cryptocurrency enforcement teams while accumulating millions with his cryptocurrency, or taking lavish gifts from foreign countries, it’s all problematic.

So, whether we’re talking about Brazil or the United States, the issue is bigger than one Instagram account or one algorithm. It’s about transparency, accountability and whether the digital platforms shaping political conversations are applying their rules fairly.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Manchin bucks Schumer, throws support behind Republican Democrats want to oust

articles.body: A top Senate Republican whom Democrats are salivating at the chance to unseat is getting an unexpected assist from a former member of their own party, delivering a political snub to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who left the Democratic Party to become an independent before retiring from the Senate, is making a swing into Maine to support Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, the lawmaker’s campaign confirmed to Fox News Digital. Collins is locked in a tight race against former Maine state Sen. Troy Jackson as she seeks a sixth term in the upper chamber. The race has remained close after it was shaken up earlier this year when Graham Platner dropped out after a sexual assault allegation rocked his campaign. 'OH, SHUT UP!': DEMOCRAT SNAPS AT COLLINS AFTER HECKLER DRIVES MAINE SENATE DEBATE OFF THE RAILS Manchin’s visit on the trail with Collins, first reported by Semafor, comes as Schumer and Democrats have tried to paint Collins as a rubber stamp for President Donald Trump, though she has often broken with the president during his second term, most notably on his signature legislation, the "one big, beautiful bill." Manchin told the outlet that his appearance alongside Collins, whom he served with during the entirety of his career in the upper chamber, was meant to demonstrate to Maine voters that Collins has a bipartisan track record that was instrumental in advancing key legislation, like his infrastructure package passed under former President Joe Biden, and blocking Trump’s policy desires, like repealing Obamacare. SCHUMER’S ‘NUMBER ONE TARGET’ SAYS VOTERS WILL SEE HER DEMOCRAT SENATE CHALLENGER AS TOO EXTREME "She is not a Trump senator," Manchin said. His foray onto the campaign trail in Maine on Wednesday will come just 24 hours before another major surrogate for Democrats will make her way to Vacationland: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Jackson has had other progressive heavyweights join him on the campaign stump, too, including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. "Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez represent the far left of the national Democratic Party," Collins spokeswoman Blake Kernen told Fox News Digital. "That they are all campaigning in Maine for Troy Jackson tells voters exactly how he would govern." SCHUMER SAYS HE'S NOT GOING ANYWHERE, BUT HIS OWN CANDIDATES AREN'T READY TO BACK HIM "Senator Manchin campaigning for Senator Collins is a testament to her record of effective, independent leadership and commitment delivering results that have greatly benefited Maine and America," she continued. Manchin’s decision to stump for Collins serves as a sharp rebuke to Schumer and the Democratic Party and comes after his years of serving as a thorn in the side of Democratic leadership and previous Democratic administrations while he was still in the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In his memoir released last year, Manchin tore into former President Barack Obama, Biden and Schumer, particularly over Schumer’s support for nuking the filibuster. That reasoning is why he wrote that he "wanted Republicans to win the Senate majority in 2024." "I believed it was the only hope for preserving the Senate as an institution," Manchin said. "I truly believed that, if in power, Republicans would uphold the filibuster, the last guardrail preventing total partisan rule."

articles.title: Trump launches women’s health initiative at National Institutes of Health
articles.summary: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday creating a task force and a National Institutes of Health division focused on women's health.
articles.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order alongside first lady Melania Trump on Monday creating a task force and a National Institutes of Health division focused on women's health. The task force will be led by Trump's White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently announced that she is cancer-free, and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a White House official said. The new Women's Health Division at NIH will not replace the agency's Office of Research on Women's Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research. "President Donald J. Trump & First Lady Melania Trump sign an executive order creating a Women's Health Division at the NIH & a White House Women's Health Task Force, aiming to close research gaps & modernize care for women," a post on X announcing the signing said. Representatives for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the NIH, could not be immediately reached for comment. The order was first reported by USA Today. In remarks at the event, Melania Trump addressed the need for using artificial intelligence to speed women's health discoveries as well as access and affordability of care. Trump and his administration have pushed for healthcare cuts, including at NIH, and last year moved to downsize the federal healthcare workforce. During Trump's second term, his administration sought to cut NIH grants for research on diversity-related topics and reportedly is moving to allow political appointees to control health-research funding. It also launched a controversial safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, that could pave the way for restrictions. Major medical groups have criticized the move as politically motivated while anti-abortion groups argue the review is moving too slowly. Earlier this month, US officials told a court the review would be completed by March. US health officials also removed a longstanding safety warning from many hormone replacement therapy products, tightening supplies and leading to shortages, and have urged more manufacturers to study testosterone therapies for women that could support future approvals of female-specific products. HHS has also targeted family planning funds, announcing earlier this year that for the first time it would require applicants for Title X funding to align their programs with Trump's political priorities, prompting legal action.

articles.title: Amanpour announces CNN departure after 43 years
articles.summary: Journalist Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s chief international anchor who has spent 43 years at the network, said Monday she will leave CNN in June 2027. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement to her employer,…
articles.body:
Journalist Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s chief international anchor who has spent 43 years at the network, said Monday she will leave CNN in June 2027.

“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement to her employer , adding that she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”

Amanpour thanked the network and the teams she has worked with since her “very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all points in between.”

CNN Chair Mark Thompson said he and Amanpour have discussed her decision to depart the outlet “for some months.”

“Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally,” Thompson said in a statement shared by CNN’s chief media analyst Brian Stelter on the social platform X .

Thompson called Amanpour “one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere” and said the network will celebrate her career at CNN before she leaves. He thanked her for “43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship.”

Amanpour has been outspoken in her concern over CNN’s future after Paramount Skydance’s bid to take over Warner Bros. Discovery, the network’s parent company. Paramount Skydance officially closed its multibillion-dollar deal to acquire Warner Bros. earlier this month, renaming the new media empire Skydance.

The CNN reporter said in May that she was “concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that he’s [Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison] taken over already, like CBS News, right? I mean do I have to list what’s happening there?”

“This ideological realignment of CBS and the destruction, potentially, of ’60 Minutes,'” Amanpour continued. “So, clearly, obviously, I’m concerned.”

Amanpour contributed to “60 Minutes” from 1996 to 2005. CNN first hired her to be part of its foreign desk in 1983, later becoming the outlet’s chief international correspondent from 1992 to 2010 and then the host of “Amanpour” beginning in 2009 on CNN International.

She had a short stint at ABC News as the anchor of “This Week” from 2010 to 2011. However, a “unique arrangement ” with ABC News allowed her to return to CNN in 2012 while continuing to work as a global affairs anchor at ABC News.

Amanpour has received several awards and honors over her career, including two George Polk Awards for Television Reporting, the Edward R. Murrow Award for Distinguished Achievement in Journalism, and the Walter Cronkite Award for Excellence in Journalism.

articles.summary: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) is the latest lawmaker to report receiving suspicious mail containing white powder in the last month. “I can confirm that my office in Leesburg received an envelope containing a suspicious substance. The office was promptly evacuated,” Subramanyam said on social platform X, adding his thanks to the Leesburg Police, Loudoun County…
articles.body:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) is the latest lawmaker to report receiving suspicious mail containing white powder in the last month.

“I can confirm that my office in Leesburg received an envelope containing a suspicious substance. The office was promptly evacuated,” Subramanyam said on social platform X , adding his thanks to the Leesburg Police, Loudoun County Fire and Rescue and hazmat team and the Capitol Police for their “swift response.”

“These acts of political intimidation have no place in our country,” he continued.

The Virginia Democrat joins dozens of lawmakers and election officials who have reported receiving similar letters containing white powder as a federal probe into the matter is reportedly underway, according to NBC News , citing a person with direct knowledge of the investigation.

Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) detailed a letter his office received that was addressed to him. His office attached a photo of the letter, containing the same return address as other letters: Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the address of a New York City building that the group listed on its membership forms.

“Needless to say, we are not involved with these letters, and we were glad to learn no one was harmed,” DSA spokesperson Priscilla Yeverino said in a statement, according to Newsweek .

“Political violence and threats of intimidation have no place in our democracy, and those responsible must be held accountable,” Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Va.) wrote after similarly reporting his district office received a letter.

GOP lawmakers have also been targeted as Sens. Pete Ricketts (Neb.), Ted Cruz (Texas) and Mike Rounds (S.D.) confirmed their district offices received letters containing a “white powder substance.”

Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry reported in an update that law enforcement found “no evidence of harmful substances” after running tests on the white powder an employee discovered when opening a package.

articles.title: Klobuchar, Demuth face off in first Minnesota governor’s debate
articles.summary: Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D) and state Rep. Lisa Demuth (R) went to bat over the budget, businesses, rising costs and the state’s fraud scandal Monday in the first debate in their race for governor. In an hourlong Monday morning program hosted by the Minnesota Chamber of Commerce, Demuth argued for a break from the…
articles.body:
Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D) and state Rep. Lisa Demuth (R) went to bat over the budget, businesses, rising costs and the state’s fraud scandal Monday in the first debate in their race for governor.

In an hourlong Monday morning program hosted by the Minnesota Chamber of Commerce, Demuth argued for a break from the status quo under Gov. Tim Walz (D), while Klobuchar distanced herself from the outgoing governor.

“We definitely need to look at what is impacting us here in the state of Minnesota because of failed Democrat leadership for far too long,” Demuth said. “Sen. Klobuchar has never once distanced herself from Gov. Walz, and every single policy that he has put in place that has increased the prices and made it harder to do business.”

“I could list a number of other ways I’m different than Tim Walz. I know you wish you were debating Tim Walz, but I’m the one here right now up here,” Klobuchar hit back.

Walz, who was Democrats’ 2024 vice presidential nominee, ultimately ended his bid for a third term as governor earlier this year amid scrutiny over a sprawling fraud scandal in the state.

Klobuchar said she “would have caught that fraud” and “done something about it” if she were in Walz’s position. And after Demuth asked why the senator didn’t “do more,” Klobuchar detailed her efforts to get more resources from the Justice Department as prosecutors probed the fraud.

A popular four-term senator and former prosecutor, Klobuchar easily won her primary and has the home-field advantage in Minnesota, where Democrats have held the governor’s mansion since 2010. Voters have rejected President Trump by single digits in each of his three elections.

But Republicans have been hopeful that the fraud scandal could open the door for a flip in the North Star State.

Trump had endorsed Republican businessman Mike Lindell, the “MyPillow Guy” who a judge ruled defamed the election tech company Smartmatic with false statements about the 2020 election, for the governor’s mansion. But Demuth, the Speaker of the state House, emerged from a crowded field to take on Klobuchar in the open race.

Cook Political Report considers the seat solidly Democratic, after shifting the race from a “likely” blue rating at the start of this year. Decision Desk HQ rates the race likely Democratic, and polling averages show Klobuchar with an 8-point lead amid a slight tightening of the race.

Both Klobuchar and Demuth said tax hikes would be off the table in their plans to balance the state’s budget and alleviate pressures on Minnesotans’ pocketbooks.

The Democrat argued that the state needs “to do something about these tariff taxes,” including negotiating subnational agreements with Canadian provinces — while Demuth has previously refrained from denouncing tariffs.

Both candidates also argued for guardrails and responsible development on artificial intelligence as debates over the rapidly developing tech and data center build-outs shape the midterms.

At one point in the debate, Demuth touted her vote in favor of the 2020 Alec Smith insulin bill in the state Legislature. But Klobuchar pointed out that Smith’s mother, Nicole Smith-Holt, has endorsed her .

“She said that my opponent, and this is a mom of a kid that died, that my opponent did not help when it comes to capping insulin. So let’s not throw that name around without being honest about the real bill that they wanted to pass,” Klobuchar said.

The gubernatorial rivals will face off again Wednesday.

articles.title: Husband of soldier killed in Iranian drone strike grills Vance on ‘fundamental failures’
articles.summary: The husband of a soldier killed in an Iranian drone strike in March grilled Vice President Vance on what he called “fundamental failures” that led up to the death of his wife. Appearing on a CBS News town hall with Vance, Joey Amor, the widower of Sgt. 1st Class Nicole Amor, detailed the drone strike…
articles.body:
The husband of a soldier killed in an Iranian drone strike in March grilled Vice President Vance on what he called “fundamental failures” that led up to the death of his wife.

Appearing on a CBS News town hall with Vance, Joey Amor, the widower of Sgt. 1st Class Nicole Amor, detailed the drone strike that killed his wife and five other soldiers.

“They raised their right hand and they gave an oath. They understood what they were doing. They understood the sacrifice that they were potentially giving,” Amor said. “Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that.”

“My wife has told me things before she passed. There are other soldiers that know things that are being quiet about certain aspects of this,” he continued, adding that “there’s a failure in the leadership, and I want to know how this administration is going to start holding those leaders accountable for the actions and the deaths of the soldiers that we honor and that we love.”

Vance told Amor this was “literally the first time I’ve heard of this.”

“This job is an amazing honor, but you live in a bit of a bubble,” he added. “That sometimes information doesn’t filter up to me, and I promise you, I will take every single failure extremely seriously, and we’ll work on it.”

The six U.S. soldiers were killed after an Iranian drone struck the tactical operations center they were working from in Kuwait; the youngest in the group was 20-year-old Sgt. Declan J. Coady.

At the time, CBS News reported the triple-wide trailer the service members were reportedly working out of was only fortified with T-walls — 12-foot-tall, steel-reinforced concrete barriers used to shield military personnel from explosions, rocket attacks and shrapnel — and that such reinforcements could not protect the trailer from an overhead strike.

Military officials also told the outlet that they did not recall hearing warning sirens prior to the strike, giving the troops no time to evacuate to a bunker.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) slammed Vance over this particular moment at the town hall, saying he “wrongly defended this war. His compassion doesn’t fix it.”

Vance’s remarks also come as he and his party are facing a rough political environment ahead of the midterms as the war effort against Iran is widely unpopular with the American public.

The Pentagon updated the American service member death toll of the Iran war to 21 earlier this month.
