articles.title: Schumer urges FCC to reject GOP group’s request to allow unsolicited political robocalls
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Monday called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to reject a petition from a conservative political group to ease restrictions on AI-generated robocalls ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and,…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Monday called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to reject a petition from a conservative political group to ease restrictions on AI-generated robocalls ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie,” Schumer said in a statement.

His warning targets a petition filed by Club for Growth, a right-leaning economic policy group, that would allow political organizations to place automated calls to cellphones without permission from recipients. The proposal would cover prerecorded messages and calls containing voices created with AI.

The New York Democrat argued that loosening the rules would make it easier for political groups to spread false information to voters through convincing AI-generated audio.

“There is absolutely no excuse to relax these standards and allow special interests to flood our cellphone ​lines with deepfakes or dark-money-funded AI voices,” Schumer said.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the FCC’s lone Democrat, echoed Schumer’s concerns, saying the senator was “right to be worried.”

“As early as this week, the FCC could unleash a flood of unwanted robocalls as voters are already inundated with this junk,” she said on the social platform X . “The last thing people want just weeks before an election is their phones overrun with AI slop.”

Gomez told CNN the FCC could make a decision in the coming days as the Nov. 3 midterms quickly approach.

But an FCC spokesperson pushed back on the possibility of an imminent approval in a statement to Reuters.

“There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving ​to an order on this or any of the petitions and there are zero plans to do so,” the spokesperson said.

Club for Growth argued that existing restrictions unfairly limit constitutionally protected political speech.

Its president, former Rep. David McIntosh (R-Ind.), said earlier this week the change would help political organizations reach and communicate with voters in a more effective way.

“Our petition asks the FCC to treat First Amendment protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, and doctor’s appointments,” McIntosh said. “We think the Constitution protects a conversation with a voter at least as highly as a delivery update.”

articles.title: Walz-era fraud scandal takes center stage as Klobuchar, GOP rival clash in debate: 'Why didn't you do more?'
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Lisa Demuth clashed over Minnesota's massive fraud scandal in their first gubernatorial debate to replace Tim Walz.
articles.body: Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth traded fire over Minnesota's massive fraud scandal as they faced off for the first time on the debate stage in the race to replace embattled Gov. Tim Walz. The race is unfolding against the backdrop of the state's welfare assistance fraud scandal, which has attracted national attention for nearly a year and prompted Walz, a two-term Democrat, to abandon his 2026 re-election bid. The fraud schemes, involving pandemic-era social services, siphoned hundreds of millions, and potentially billions, of taxpayer dollars from federal and state programs in Minnesota. Demuth is aiming to become the first Republican in twenty years to win a gubernatorial election in the blue-leaning Midwestern state. Polls indicate Klobuchar holding an upper single digit lead over Demuth, and the Fox News Power Rankings rate the race Likely Democrat. Demuth, during the first half of the debate, repeatedly steered the conversation to the fraud scandal. FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD "We have allowed a culture of waste and fraud to go on far too long and we can’t keep going this way," she said, as she worked to link Klobuchar to Walz, who has taken full responsibility for the scandal. "Klobuchar, referring to Walz, said, "I have been very clear. I would have caught that fraud. I would have done something about it. We have very different backgrounds." Demuth asked her rival, "You could have reached out to the governor and said I think we have a problem in Minnesota... Why didn't you do more." And Demuth asked, "Why weren’t you at the hearings about fraud in your own Senate Judicial Committee hearing when we had Minnesotans who were concerned about fraud." FORMER NFL SIDELINE REPORTER PUTS MINNESOTA'S SENATE SEAT IN PLAY FOR REPUBLICANS Klobuchar, pushing back, highlighted that "the minute that the fraud went public, I did something that was real….. I called the justice department and asked for more resources. The senator said her actions led to more federal prosecutors assigned to investigate the fraud scandal. "That’s doing the real work," she emphasized. Responding to Demuth's claims of missing hearings, which Fox News Digital reported on earlier this year, Klobuchar said, "I’ve been at a dozen hearings where I’ve raised or asked questions about fraud. The particular hearing that was raised here was a subcommittee that I was not even on." Demuth also pledged to fire "all of the commissioners in the state of Minnesota" in order to start "fresh" after the fraud scandal. The two candidates also sparred over healthcare, with Demuth pointing to Klobuchar's support of ObamaCare as being tied to the rising healthcare costs in the state. "We must recognize that our healthcare costs have exploded across the country and in Minnesota because of the Affordable Care Act," Demuth said. "The senator said that it would bring the cost of our healthcare down, we could access whatever we needed and it would be more affordable. That is absolutely untrue where we find ourselves today." The two candidates, in what was billed as a business forum hosted by the Minnesota Chamber of Commerce, also took aim at each other over high gas prices, healthcare, paid family and medical leave, and efforts to cap insulin costs. On state taxes, both seemed in agreement. "Tax hikes are absolutely off the table for me," Demuth emphasized. Klobuchar said, "I’ve made clear I’m not going to increase taxes." And she touted, "I’ve been willing to take on my own party on taxes in the past." Klobuchar launched her gubernatorial campaign in January, three weeks after Walz, who served as the Democrats' 2024 vice presidential nominee, dropped his re-election bid. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Klobuchar, who was first elected to the Senate in 2006, won all four of her Senate elections by healthy margins, including a nearly 16-point re-election in 2024. Before serving in the Senate, Klobuchar was elected twice as county attorney in Hennepin County, Minnesota's most populous. She also ran unsuccessfully for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination. She captured nearly 90% of the vote in the August Democratic primary against a large field of longshot rivals. Demuth, who was first elected to the Minnesota House in 2018, has served as GOP leader in the chamber since the start of 2023 and as speaker for the past year and a half, In the GOP gubernatorial primary, Demuth topped a crowded field, defeated by 11-points second place finisher Mike Lindell, the My Pillow founder and former CEO who is a close ally of President Donald Trump and who joined the president in denying former President Joe Biden's victory in the 2020 White House race. Trump endorsed Lindell a month before the August 11 primary.

articles.body:
Jon Stewart is staying with “The Daily Show” through the next White House race.

Comedy Central announced Monday that Stewart will extend his once-a-week hosting duties through December 2028.

The 63-year-old comedian hosts “The Daily Show” on Mondays and also serves as its executive producer. A rotating lineup of comics and TV personalities host the show through the rest of the week.

“Jon Stewart is a generational talent and ‘The Daily Show’ continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central,” George Cheeks, Skydance TV’s co-chair and chief content officer, said in a statement.

“We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award-winning news team,” Cheeks said.

Stewart hosted “The Daily Show” full time for 16 years before stepping down in 2015. He returned to the satirical news program for his Monday night hosting gig in 2024. At the time, the network hailed the Emmy winner’s homecoming, calling him the “perfect person to puncture the empty rhetoric and provide much-needed clarity with his brilliant wit” in “our age of staggering hypocrisy and performative politics.”

Last year, Comedy Central announced Stewart had inked a new deal to keep him in the hosting chair through 2026.

articles.body:
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told senators Ukraine still does not have full access to the critical satellite-based Starshield network or U.S. intelligence sharing amid growing tensions with President Trump.

Zelensky provided the update to a bipartisan group of senators on a call hosted by Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

“Joined Senator Tillis today to host an update from President Zelenskyy with bipartisan colleagues—hearing from him highly alarmingly that intelligence sharing & Starshield access are still partially degraded,” Blumenthal posted on the social platform X .

Blumenthal said Democratic and Republican senators are preparing to act immediately to signal their displeasure that the Trump administration hasn’t given Ukraine the same access to intelligence and internet connectivity, which is crucial to operating drones and other military vehicles, as it had at the start of October.

“President Zelenskyy is ready for a mutual ceasefire on energy facilities & resources, & civilians, if only Putin will agree. Vicious, bloodthirsty slaughter by Russia’s missiles & drones is intensifying,” Blumenthal said.

“Bipartisan, bicameral support for Ukraine was clear & unequivocal, which we’ll be expressing in upcoming action,” he added.

Reports last week that Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, was substantially restricted caused an uproar among Republican and Democratic lawmakers.

Four GOP senators signed onto a bipartisan letter last week to Platte Moring, the Defense Department’s inspector general, demanding an investigation into whether senior Pentagon officials , including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, ordered or had advance knowledge of restrictions on Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield.

The senators also warned that Ukraine’s loss of access to U.S. intelligence may have put American diplomatic, security and military personnel on the ground in Ukraine in danger.

Former Ukraine Minister of Defense Mykhailo Fedorov announced Wednesday that Ukraine’s connectivity with Starlink was being restored at speeds of up to 160 km per hour, helping it to operate military vehicles flying at that speed, suggesting that service had been restored.

But Zelensky told senators more recently that the speeds are still lagging.

The loss of full satellite network access and U.S. intelligence sharing comes as Trump appears increasingly frustrated by Ukraine’s strikes on Russian petroleum facilities.

“Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States,” Trump posted Sunday on Truth Social.

“Farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World. Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war,” Trump added.

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: Senate sneaks in one last political play before voters have their say
articles.summary: Senate Republicans forced a vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act to curb data center utility costs, but Democrats call it a toothless political ploy.
articles.body: In politics, you sometimes just do what you can. All 100 duly chosen and sworn U.S. senators understood why the Senate met for a week at the end of September. Yes there was the college sports bill. Yes there was the confirmation of Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling. Yes there was a big hearing with former special counsel Jack Smith. But you’d be badly mistaken if you thought both sides were really there to hammer out a package to bring down the cost of living for Americans. Don’t take my word for it. Take the word of the senators. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: A GUIDE TO THE COLLEGE SPORTS VOTE AND SENATE’S OHIO SHOWDOWN You are correct to say that Democrats blocked two bills that Republicans say voters really want. One was a measure to diminish the costs consumers pay for data centers and a plan to restrict stock trades by lawmakers. The latter bill even included a voter ID requirement – crucial to the GOP and its base. But Republican senators knew that Democrats wouldn’t accept these proposals. This was about politics. And Democratic senators wouldn’t accept any of the GOP’s legislative propositions, either. So let’s start with the Ratepayer Protection Act. Both sides know that voters are tripped out about AI and utterly losing it when it comes to data centers. An internal GOP memo in August revealed that the party was especially leery of what this meant for Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine appointed Husted to the Senate last year to succeed Vice President JD Vance. Husted helped foster development of data centers as an official back in the Buckeye State. So, the final week of the Senate’s session before the midterms crawled with politics. REPUBLICANS FEAR THEY ‘HAVEN’T DONE A DAMN THING’ TO LOWER PRICES AHEAD OF MIDTERM RECKONING Republicans aimed to curb skyrocketing utility costs associated with the construction of data centers. "(People) ought to be guaranteed no electricity bills will go up by a cent because of a data center," said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. "It sends a clear message that these AI companies and these data centers can't just come into local communities and strip mine out (land). Raise the electricity rates. Kick people off the grid. Take their water." But Democrats say the bill didn’t compel compliance by AI firms. This was just a suggestion that those who build the data centers help foot some of the bill. "It is a sham. A charade because it has no enforcement," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. "Everything in that bill can already be done by a state regulator. Or it can already be done by a data center developer. And the bill requires nothing of them," argued Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. I pressed Kaine on if "something was better than nothing." He disagreed. "No. You shouldn't trick people. And this is not even something," replied Kaine. "It's nothing," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., piled on with, "The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill." The bill is laced with midterm politics. Democrats claim Republicans called the vote to throw a lifeline to Husted. Many Senate Republicans were ready for the Senate to leave town for the midterms. But they hedged their bets around the data center bill. And, Husted. "Can you say 110 precent this is not a vote to help Jon Husted in Ohio?" yours truly inquired of Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D. "I think it will help him," replied Hoeven. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., agreed with Hoeven. "The one thing I'll just say is that this is clearly a political ploy," said Kim. "This is not something that's good for the American people. But it's certainly good for Sen. Husted." DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS The tilt between Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, is one of the nation’s most contentious Senate contests. "I don't think that there's a secret that Sen. Husted is trying to pass a piece of legislation so he could go home and run a campaign ad," said Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M. Husted conceded as much. "We gave everybody a chance to do something about affordability and the Democrats blocked it. So we'll go campaign on it," said Husted. So yes. The Senate’s last week of session was about the midterms. "Has there ever been a late September or October before an election that wasn't all politics?" asked Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. The evolving positions on the data center bill by Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., may be an example of that. Welch was a yea when asked about the legislation on September 23 , after it overwhelmingly cleared the House. "I support it and I'd be glad to vote on it," said Welch. But the Vermont Democrat flipped to nay when the issue approached a roll call vote on the floor. "Why did you change? I asked Welch. "Well, two things. One, they won't allow us to have an amendment. And the problem with this bill is that it has no teeth," he replied. So the question is whether the sides prefer action. Or, if they’d rather have the issue. In fact it could be argued that Husted may have scored some political capital, deploying the blocked bill as a foil in an effort to contrast himself to Democrats. "It ought to be something that should be a no brainer here on the floor of the Senate," said Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS' It’s rare that competitive Senate contests pivot on a solitary issue. And certainly an individual debate or vote. Democratic Maine Senate nominee Troy Jackson is pushing Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, on her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh in 2018. It was one of the most factious confirmation battles in history. But Collins won reelection in 2020. That vote was eight years ago. A vote like the one on the data center measure just before the election can plant a seed in the mind of voters. And since Republicans were struggling on affordability – and then AI and data centers emerged as an issue – forcing this vote was probably the best political play the GOP had at its disposal. In campaigns, you do all you can. Let’s say for a moment that Husted loses narrowly to Brown in two weeks. And maybe Republicans would have held the Senate had Husted prevailed. Perhaps exit polling reveals that voters wished Republicans had done more on affordability. Party insiders would then accuse the Senate GOP brass of political malpractice by denying Husted a chance to make his case. It was the best Husted could do. And the best Senate Republicans could do. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It may not work. But at least Republicans can say they did what they could.

articles.title: Smithsonian screening dispute puts museum's commitment to diverse views on trial: 'Right kind of Black?'
articles.summary: The Smithsonian National Museum of African American History declined a public screening of "White Guilt," a documentary by filmmaker Eli Steele.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — A Black conservative filmmaker is challenging the Smithsonian to explain why his documentary questioning progressive views on race has yet to secure a public screening at its African American history museum, which has previously showcased films examining systemic racism. "White Guilt," directed and co-produced by Eli Steele, is based on a book by his father, noted Black conservative academic Shelby Steele. The younger Steele, who is Black, Jewish and deaf, has drawn on his own experiences to challenge prevailing views on race and identity. The documentary argues that White guilt over America's racial history, along with fears of being labeled racist, has pushed institutions to prioritize racial identity over individual merit. The dispute comes as the Smithsonian faces mounting pressure from President Donald Trump and his administration over allegations of ideological bias in its portrayal of American history. The White House has accused the institution of promoting progressive narratives and threatened to restrict federal support, escalating a broader battle over whose perspectives are represented in the nation's museums. SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES Steele provided communications to Fox News Digital showing that the museum declined his proposed screening dates and offered him a private rental option instead. The filmmaker says the museum has yet to respond to his request for alternative dates for a public screening. "The film is professionally shot, the quality is there. A comparable film that they've shown is '13th,' which itself is a very controversial film," Steele told Fox News Digital. "So that's the big question we have here: Do we have viewpoint diversity or do we not? Do you have to be the right kind of Black to be shown at the Smithsonian?" "That's the big question that we have to address in this room. But I hope that it's not about any of that," he continued. The filmmaker has questioned the apparent decision to not screen his film, given that the museum has allowed numerous other films with more progressive messages to have public screenings, though stopped short of accusing the museum of ideological discrimination. "13th," the film mentioned by Steele, is featured in educational and public programming at the NMAAHC. It argues that the 13th Amendment’s exception permitting forced labor as punishment for a crime enabled racial control to persist after slavery by allegedly criminalizing Black behavior. Other films shown by the NMAAHC in public screenings include such titles as "Hidden Figures" in 2016, "I Am Not Your Negro" in 2017 and "Faith in Blackness: An Exploration of AfroLatine Spirituality" in 2023, the latter presented in partnership with the Smithsonian Folklife Festival. LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT While Steele was hesitant to speculate as to why his film hadn't been scheduled for a public screening, other Black conservatives saw the museum's handling of his request as part of a familiar pattern. "Academia is not what it was years ago when I went to graduate school, when it touted itself as a marketplace for ideas," Carol Swain, a retired Black conservative professor and prominent media commentator, told Fox News Digital. "There would always be a token conservative included. And I have found over the years that conservatives were tolerated less and less. And if they were black, at some point they were not tolerated at all." "When you look at an institution like the Smithsonian, that's supposed to belong to all of us, to all Americans, you would think that it would be open to divergent views," Swain, who spent her career at institutions such as Princeton and Vanderbilt, continued. "That is not what we find." Wall Street Journal columnist and Manhattan Institute senior fellow Jason Riley shared a similar perspective. FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM "I think the type of people who run the Smithsonian Institute are part of the broader liberal intelligentsia in this country that prevails in academia, prevails and the media. And this is not a point of view. That they take kindness to," Riley told Fox News Digital. "In fact, this film takes some rather direct shots at that group of people. So there might be some self-interest here. It might cut a little too close to these folks." "I do think that they have a vested interest in putting forward a narrative out there to advance a political agenda. And I think that's what's really going on here at places like the Smithsonian," Riley continued, citing his experience as a Black commentator who has spent his career sparring with White liberals. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED Both Riley and Swain argued that viewing the film could do a service to White progressives by challenging their assumptions about race and forcing them to confront whether their preferred policies are actually helping Black America. Riley stated that the Black Americans who regularly attend the NMAAHC could benefit from Steele’s film as it challenges the popular assumption that they are blocked from social mobility by virtue of their race. In recent months, the Smithsonian has been the target of criticism from Republican elected officials, including the president, who argue that the institution has allowed political bias to overshadow the neutral presentation of history, an argument some within the organization reject, claiming that they are simply presenting the good and the bad aspects of the American story. As part of its effort to pressure the Smithsonian over what it describes as ideological bias, the Trump administration has threatened to restrict federal support, including discretionary grants and cooperation from federal agencies. While Riley and Swain raised questions about the Smithsonian's motives, the museum told Steele that his proposed dates were unavailable but did not explain whether it would consider alternative dates for a public screening, according to correspondence reviewed by Fox News Digital. Steele and his team reached out to the Smithsonian in late August about a public screening of their film, receiving a response within the day directing them to fill out an event application form, according to correspondence reviewed by Fox News Digital. In early September, they submitted a completed application form and provided two possible dates for a screening. About two weeks later, the NMAAHC responded by informing them that neither date was available for a public screening, according to the correspondence. After Steele's team asked about alternatives, the museum offered them the option of renting space for a private screening at a quoted cost of $35,000, according to correspondence reviewed by Fox News Digital, rather than arranging a museum-sponsored public screening. INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION When Steele and his team clarified that they wanted a public screening and signaled flexibility on their requested dates, they received no response from the museum, per correspondence reviewed by Fox News Digital. "Answering email does not take that much time," Steele told Fox News Digital. "I watched the film last night. It's a well-made and powerful representation of ideas that Shelby Steele has been developing over the last 40 years," Glenn Loury, an African American professor at Brown University who has described himself as "conservative-leaning," told Fox News Digital. "Those ideas — about how racial identity interacts with the pursuit of ‘black power’ and the quest for ‘white innocence’ in the West — are vividly illuminated through the film's exploration of a number of exemplary cases." "The arguments advanced via Steele's eloquent narration in the film are not beyond questioning, but they are invariably provocative and insightful," he continued. "It would certainly be an appropriate use of the platform of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture to screen this documentary, as a means of provoking critical engagement with its themes from all corners of the political/ideological spectrum." IN PICTURES: HISTORIC SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM PACKED WITH WOKE POLITICAL MESSAGING ON RACE AND GENDER NMAAHC did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital. "My father, Shelby Steele, was born into segregation and has spent decades examining how America has changed, how far we have come, and what still divides us. ‘White Guilt,’ drawing on his 2006 book, brings that work to the screen," Steele said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "We approached the Smithsonian’s African American museum because we believe that conversation belongs there. Sharing his life’s work in a museum dedicated to the history he lived would mean a great deal to both of us." articles.title: Hinojosa sues to review confidential emails between Musk, Abbott
articles.summary: The communications were deemed confidential due to their “embarrassing” and “intimate” nature.
articles.body:
AUSTIN (Nexstar) — State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for Texas governor, is suing her gubernatorial opponent in order to review more than a thousand pages of communication between Greg Abbott’s office and Elon Musk’s representatives, which were deemed confidential due to their “embarrassing” and “intimate” nature.

“Nobody here is accusing Greg Abbott of having a torrid love affair with Elon Musk,” said Hinojosa in front of the Travis County courthouse Monday morning. “What this is about is we have the world’s only trillionaire getting massive tax breaks from this governor after giving him over $500,000 in campaign contributions.”

Nexstar reached out to the governor’s office for comment on this story, and is waiting to hear back.

The documents Hinojosa is after were part of a public records request filed by The Texas Newsroom in 2025. The governor’s office objected to releasing the communications on several grounds, including “the state’s competitive business interests, attorney-client privilege, and deliberative-process privilege,” according to Hinojosa’s lawsuit.

In August 2025, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sustained the objections but directed the governor’s office to release some of the requested materials. The governor’s office produced 1,374 pages to the Texas Newsroom, but only around 200 pages were not redacted, according to the lawsuit.

Hinojosa wrote a letter to the governor’s office on Sep. 29 requesting to review the redacted information and cited a Texas law that allows members of the legislature to review confidential documents for “legislative purposes.”

However, Hinojosa could be required to sign a confidentiality agreement that would bar her from speaking about the content in the documents publicly. She offered to sign such an agreement in her letter to Abbott.

“The people of Texas and the people of House District 49 are concerned over the growing power of tech giants in Texas regarding our tax dollars, resources, and data,” reads Hinojosa’s letter. “In light of the expanding influence of tech CEOs in Texas and the close working relationship between government and the corporate tech industry, transparency is essential for accountability, which is why I’m writing.”

Hinojosa said she received a letter from Abbott’s office denying her request, according to the lawsuit.

Musk has multiple companies stationed in Texas, including SpaceX, Starlink, Tesla, X, The Boring Company, Neuralink, and xAI. Musk also contributed $500,000 to Abbott’s campaign, along with another $250,000 contribution to Speaker of the Texas House Dustin Burrows, in 2026, according to records from the Texas Ethics Commission.

“People have a right to know, and I, as their representative, have the right to see them,” Hinojosa said.

In her filing, Hinojosa lists examples of Musk’s companies receiving grants and tax breaks from Texas, including:

A $1.7 billion school property tax incentive for Musk’s Terafab project through the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program

$17.3 million grant for SpaceX in Bastrop on March 12, 2025

$7.5 million grant from the Texas Space Commission for SpaceX and its Starbase operations in Brownsville on Feb. 10, 2025

Hinojosa is requesting a temporary restraining order to prohibit the governor’s office from blocking her access to the documents.

articles.title: Congress colleagues, former rivals: Bains gets 1 year in jail for defaming Mohindra
articles.summary: Patiala court sentences ex-MLA Simarjeet Bains to 1 year rigorous jail for defaming ex-Punjab health minister Brahm Mohindra over corruption claims.
articles.body: Patiala: A Patiala court on Monday sentenced former MLA Simarjit Singh Bains to one year’s rigorous imprisonment for criminal defamation over allegations of corruption against former Punjab health minister Brahm Mohindra, following an eight-year legal battle.Chief judicial magistrate Ekta Sahota convicted Bains under Section 500 of the IPC, holding that he had failed to substantiate his allegations against Mohindra, now his Congress colleague. Bains, who headed the Lok Insaaf Party before merging it into the Congress ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, had accused Mohindra of secretly owning a pharmaceutical firm and running a “medicines mafia” that coerced de-addiction centres into buying drugs from it.He had also alleged that Mohindra used officials to threaten nearly 80 private rehabilitation centres with licence cancellations and manipulated medicine tender conditions to favour multinational companies.Mohindra, then health and family welfare minister, had challenged Bains to provide evidence or apologise before initiating criminal proceedings in August 2018.The court said Bains had produced no evidence to support his corruption allegations or establish that he had acted in good faith and in the public interest. It held that freedom of speech could not override another person’s right to reputation and dignity.During the trial, 23 witnesses were examined, including drug licensing officials, health department administrators, cybercrime personnel and media record-keepers. Records showed the pharmaceutical firm had no commercial or financial links with Mohindra.Bains’s counsel argued that he had acted as a political whistleblower and challenged the admissibility of electronic evidence. The court rejected the arguments.Bains sought leniency, citing his role as his family’s sole breadwinner and the prolonged trial. The court said the seriousness of the allegations warranted the sentence.
